    Personal Guidance
    Sañjaya describes: having said this, the great Lord, the master of all yogic mysteries, displayed His universal form to Arjuna.
    Practical Applications
    • Receive Sañjaya's narration as the lens through which we still see this scene.
    • Honor the messenger who relays the scene.
    • Don't skip narrators in your reading.
    Reflection Questions
    • What narrators of the spiritual scene am I ignoring?
    • What does honoring them open?
    Analogy

    When the curtain rises, the narrator's voice fills in what no actor can show: who is speaking, in what register, to whom. Sañjaya is that narrator, and his single sentence — evam uktvā, having spoken thus — frames the entire vision that follows.

    Stories
    Sañjaya's Reporting Voice

    Throughout the Bhagavad-gītā, Sañjaya appears only at hinge moments — opening verse, the divya-cakṣus granted at the start, and again here at the unveiling of the universal form (Mahābhārata, Bhīṣma-parva).

    His voice in 11.9 — mahā-yogeśvaro hariḥ — is doing theological work. He names Kṛṣṇa as both Hari and the great Lord of yoga, telling Dhṛtarāṣṭra (and us) the identity of the speaker before the form is described. Without this introduction, the wonders that follow could be misread as deva-līlā.

    Important Words
    • aneka — many
      Repeated four times in two verses. Sañjaya's vocabulary breaks down under the pressure of plurality — he can only keep saying aneka, aneka, aneka.
    • vaktra — mouths
      Mouths in particular, because the mouths will become terrible in verses 25–30 — the same vaktras that now hold garlands will later devour kings. The seed of the awful is in the wonderful.
    • divya — divine, celestial
      Used four times — for ornaments, weapons, garments, garments-and-fragrances. Everything Arjuna sees is divya; the material register has been suspended.
    • udyata — upraised
      Past participle of ud-yam, 'to lift.' The weapons are not at rest — they are raised, in active readiness. Even at this descriptive moment, the form is implicitly about to act.
    • anantam — unlimited
      Neuter singular, agreeing with devam. Sañjaya's last word in the description: after every count and catalogue, the only honest adjective is 'limitless.'
    • viśvataḥ - mukham — facing all directions
      Compound: 'with mouth(s) on every side.' The Lord has no front and no back; every approach meets a face. This will become Arjuna's terror in verse 24.
    Arjuna saw in that universal form unlimited mouths, unlimited eyes, unlimited wonderful visions. The form was decorated with many celestial ornaments and bore many divine upraised weapons. He wore celestial garlands and garments, and many divine scents were smeared over His body. All was wondrous, brilliant, unlimited, all-expanding.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Sañjaya pauses on the first impression: not yet terror, but vertiginous abundance. Every feature is multiplied — mouths, eyes, ornaments, weapons — and every direction is a face. The viśvarūpa announces itself first as overwhelming opulence before it turns to its devouring aspect.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    A dual-verse Upajāti unit dense with prefix 'aneka' (many) and 'divya' (divine) — the form is both quantitatively and qualitatively beyond the human. 'Viśvato-mukham' picks up the Vedic image (Puruṣa-sūkta, RV 10.90) of the cosmic Person whose face is everywhere. The catalog is deliberately impersonal in number to mark its incomparability with any deva-icon.

    Purport

    In these two verses the repeated use of the word many indicates that there was no limit to the number of hands, mouths, legs and other manifestations Arjuna was seeing. These manifestations were distributed throughout the universe, but by the grace of the Lord, Arjuna could see them while sitting in one place. That was due to the inconceivable potency of Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    10. It had many mouths and eyes, many astonishing aspects, many wonderful ornaments, uplifting many wonderful weapons. 11. That form wore astonishing garlands and dress, astonishing perfumes and ointments. It was shining, greatly amazing, infinite, with faces in every direction.
    Commentary

    Viśvato mukham means “whose faces are everywhere.”

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    10. It had many mouths and eyes, many astonishing aspects, many wonderful ornaments, uplifting many wonderful weapons. 11. That form wore astonishing garlands and dress, astonishing ointments and fragrances. It was shining, greatly amazing, beyond compare, with faces in every direction.
    Commentary

    That form had thousands (aneka) of mouths and eyes, since later there is a description of the form with thousands of arms: sahasra-bāho bhava viśva-mūrte (BG 11.46) The use of the word aneka here indicates that the arms and eyes were so numerous that they could not be counted (instead of just several, which is the other meaning of aneka.) This is understood from the śruti statement viśvataś cakṣur uta viśvatomukhaḥ: His eyes are everywhere, His faces are everywhere. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.3) In that form he saw many astonishing things (anekādbhuta darśanam).

    That form had celestial fragrances and ointments. It was shining (devam), unprecedented (anantam), and had faces in all directions (viśvato mukham).

This whole portion is connected with the verb '(He) showed' in the earlier verse. Moreover,
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation

'Anantam' (boundless) means that form is not limited by time and space because of its being the foundation of the entire universe in the past, present and future.     Personal Guidance
    Arjuna saw unlimited mouths, unlimited eyes, unlimited wonderful visions, weapons, garlands, anointed with celestial perfumes — all wonderful, brilliant, unlimited.
    Practical Applications
    • Don't reduce the universal form to symbol; the verse says actual unlimited features.
    • Honor the multisensory richness of the vision.
    • Cultivate the imagination to receive scriptural description.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I reduced spiritual reality to mere symbol?
    • What imaginative receptivity is being asked?
    Analogy

    Imagine a king's coronation portrait: every ornament catalogued, every weapon held aloft, every fragrance noted. The catalogue itself is the portrait. So Sañjaya, unable to paint, lists — and the list becomes the form.

    Stories
    Markaṇḍeya in the Belly of Viṣṇu

    When the sage Markaṇḍeya was swept into the cosmic waters of dissolution (Mahābhārata, Vana-parva 188–189; Bhāgavatam 12.9), he wandered inside the body of the Supreme Lord and saw the same kinds of marvels Arjuna now sees — unlimited mouths, eyes, ornaments, weapons, garlands, all radiant beyond measure.

    The Gītā's description in 11.10–11 echoes Markaṇḍeya's seeing. The viśva-rūpa is not a one-off display for a battlefield; it is the standing truth, occasionally unveiled to a few prepared souls.

    Important Words
    • divi — in the sky
      Locative. Sañjaya situates the imagined sunrise in the divya realm, not in the earth's atmosphere. The comparison is cosmic, not meteorological.
    • sūrya — of suns
      Genitive in compound with sahasrasya. The sun, the most luminous object known to ordinary experience, is multiplied — and even multiplied a thousandfold, only approximates.
    • sahasrasya — of a thousand
      Genitive singular. Sanskrit often uses sahasra as 'innumerable.' Even 'a thousand' here is a polite under-count.
    • yugapat — all at once
      Adverb — 'at the same instant.' The full force is in the simultaneity. A sun rising over many hours does not match; a thousand suns rising at the same instant might.
    • sadṛśī — similar
      Feminine adjective (qualifying bhāḥ, light). Sañjaya carefully does not say 'equal.' Even the most extreme analogy is only sadṛśī, similar — and only might be.
    • mahā - ātmanaḥ — of the great Self
      Genitive of mahātman. The brightness belongs to the mahātman; the suns are merely the measuring rod. The genitive keeps possession clear.
    If hundreds of thousands of suns were to rise at once into the sky, their radiance might resemble the effulgence of the Supreme Person in that universal form.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    A famous similitude: a thousand suns simultaneously rising only approach the splendor of the cosmic Person. The optative stack ('bhavet … syāt') is humble — even the analogy is conjectural; nothing in nature directly matches what Arjuna now sees.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Echoed by J. Robert Oppenheimer at Trinity (1945): 'If the radiance of a thousand suns…' The image dramatizes that the viśvarūpa is not just visually large but is sheer light beyond luminance. 'Mahātmā' here means the cosmic Self, not (as in moral usage) a great soul. Compare Muṇḍaka 2.2.10: 'na tatra sūryo bhāti.'

    Purport

    What Arjuna saw was indescribable, yet Sañjaya is trying to give a mental picture of that great revelation to Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Neither Sañjaya nor Dhṛtarāṣṭra was present, but Sañjaya, by the grace of Vyāsa, could see whatever happened. Thus he now compares the situation, as far as it can be understood, to an imaginable phenomenon (i.e., thousands of suns).

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    12. If the splendor of a thousand suns rose simultaneously in the sky, that effulgence would be somewhat similar to the effulgence of this great form.
    Commentary

    If at one time the effulgence (bhāḥ) of a thousand suns arose, then it would be somewhat similar to the effulgence (bhāsaḥ) of the universal form (mahātmanaḥ).

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    12. If the splendor of a thousand suns rose simultaneously in the sky, that effulgence would be similar to one of the splendors in the effulgence of this great form.
    Commentary

    This verse described the incomparable effulgence of that form. If the effulgence of a thousand suns rose in the sky at once, it would be similar to one of the splendors of this universal form (mahāṭmanaḥ) of the Lord. Optative tense is used to show supposition. Here a metaphor called utprekṣa or poetic fancy is used, comparing the effulgence of a thousand suns to the astonishing nature of the object of comparison, the universal form. But since the comparison is deficient, what is suggested is that nothing could compare to this form’s effulgence. The verse is a continuation of the thought expressed previously in verse 9: He showed that form.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Because the magninimity or the greatness of the universal form was so wondrous and brilliant, unlimiting, all expanding, it is impossible to conceive of something like that. Here an example is given to give us some idea of the radiance of this form: 'If hundreds of thousands of suns were to rise at once into the sky'.

    Personal Guidance
    If hundreds of thousands of suns rose at once, their splendor might approach the splendor of that Supreme Personality.
    Practical Applications
    • Hold the magnitude — many suns' splendor.
    • Use this image to dwarf personal worries.
    • Recognize that the Lord's brilliance is beyond ordinary measurement.
    Reflection Questions
    • What worry of mine fits 'a single sun'-sized perspective?
    • How does the magnitude shift it?
    Analogy

    If a thousand suns were to rise together — that's the only handhold the mind is given. Even then it is a similitude, not the thing. The verse trains the disciple to compare and then to confess the comparison is inadequate.

    Stories
    Bhīṣma sees the Light of lights

    On the bed of arrows, with Kṛṣṇa standing before him whip in hand, Bhīṣma offered the Bhīṣma-stuti (Bhāgavatam 1.9). He did not address an impersonal radiance; he addressed Pārtha-sārathi — the dark-bodied charioteer whose face was reddened with battle-dust — and called Him the source of all light, the very person on whom yogīs meditate.

    This is the light the Gītā names at 13.18 as jyotiṣām api taj jyotiḥ — the Light beyond all lights. Kṛṣṇa now shows Arjuna the upper limit of that effulgence: a thousand suns, and even those only might resemble it (sadṛśī syāt).

    Important Words
    • eka - stham — in one place
      Same compound as 11.7 — the verse rhymes with Kṛṣṇa's earlier promise. What was offered there is now received here.
    • jagat — the universe
      The moving world. Even in its perpetual motion, it is held in one place by the Lord — motion does not contradict locus.
    • pravibhaktam — divided
      Past passive participle of pra-vi-bhaj — 'split apart in many directions.' Multiplicity is real, but it is held within unity, not opposed to it.
    • anekadhā — in many ways
      Adverb. Not just 'many,' but 'many-fold' — distributed across innumerable modes. The Gītā does not erase difference; it situates it.
    • deva - devasya — of the Lord of lords
      Genitive compound. The body in which all this is held is itself the body of the deva-deva — not merely a great being but the source of greatness.
    At that time Arjuna could see in the universal form of the Lord the unlimited expansions of the universe situated in one place although divided into many, many thousands.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण
    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    The promise of 11.7 ('eka-sthaṁ jagat kṛtsnam') is fulfilled in perception. Arjuna sees a paradoxical object: a manifold endlessly diverse and yet co-present in a single body. Multiplicity and unity coincide without contradiction.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The verse names the central metaphysical demonstration of the chapter — non-dual diversity. 'Pravibhaktam anekadhā' and 'eka-stham' are deliberately yoked. The narrator calls Arjuna 'Pāṇḍava' (lineage-name) just here, perhaps to mark the historic uniqueness of the moment within his lineage's story; cf. 11.47-48.
    Prose order (अन्वय · Anvaya)
    तदा पाण्डवः तत्र देव-देवस्य शरीरे अनेकधा प्रविभक्तं कृत्स्नं जगत् एक-स्थम् अपश्यत् ।
    tadā pāṇḍavaḥ tatra deva-devasya śarīre anekadhā pravibhaktaṃ kṛtsnaṃ jagat eka-stham apaśyat |
    Then the son of Pāṇḍu saw there, in the body of the God of gods, the entire universe — divided manifold yet gathered in one place.

    Purport

    The word tatra (“there”) is very significant. It indicates that both Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa were sitting on the chariot when Arjuna saw the universal form. Others on the battlefield could not see this form, because Kṛṣṇa gave the vision only to Arjuna. Arjuna could see in the body of Kṛṣṇa many thousands of planets. As we learn from Vedic scriptures, there are many universes and many planets. Some of them are made of earth, some are made of gold, some are made of jewels, some are very great, some are not so great, etc. Sitting on his chariot, Arjuna could see all these. But no one could understand what was going on between Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    13. On the battlefield, Arjuna saw parts of the universe in various parts of that body in various ways.
    Commentary

    In that place (tatra), on the battle field, in the body of the Lord (deva-devasya), it was impossible to take into account the whole universe. Therefore Arjuna saw a part situated in one part of the body at different moments (pravibhaktam, eka-stham)—a part situated in the Lord’s pore or a part situated in His belly, and in various ways (anekadhā). That is, he saw that form made of earth, made of gold, made of jewels, or measuring fifty koṭi yojanas, or a hundred koṭi yojanas or a hundred thousand koṭi yojanas.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    13. On the battlefield, in the body of the Lord, Arjuna then saw parts of the whole universe in one place in various ways.
    Commentary

    Then what happened? There, on the battlefield (tatra), in the body of Kṛṣṇa (devadevasya) with a thousand heads, in that sacred form, Arjuna then saw the whole universe, all its various parts (pravibhaktam) in one place (ekastham), as was explained already in verse 7. The universe was variously composed of earth, gold, and jewels (anekadhā). Or it can mean that the universe appeared in small, medium and large forms.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Arjuna saw all the different universes with many sizes and many ingredients all in one place and also in their own separate existence.

    [2. Krsna's universal form of opulences: Arjuna, with hair standing on end, bewildered and astonished, prays, "My dear Krsna, I see all demigods, sages, and serpents within Your fiery form. You are the all‑pervading, eternal Personality of Godhead. The sun and the moon are eyes and Your glory is unlimited. You are burning the universe by Your radiance. (14‑19) ]

He beheld 'the whole universe' with all its sub-divisions, differentiated into varied and wonderful classes of experiencing beings like Brahma, gods, animals, men, immovables etc., and the places, objects and means of experiences such as earth, ether, Rasatala, Atala, Vitala, Sutala etc. He beheld thus the entire universe as depicted in such texts as those starting with 'I am the origin of all; from Me proceed everything' (10.8), 'Indeed I shall tell you, O Arjuna, My glorious self-manifestations' (10.9), 'I am the Self, O Arjuna, dwelling in the hearts of all beings' (10.20), and 'Of Adityas, I am Visnu' (10.21), and ending with 'Nothing that moves or does not move exists without Me' (10.39), and 'I remain, with a single fraction of Myself sustaining this whole universe' (10.42).

    Personal Guidance
    At that time Arjuna could see in the universal form the unlimited expansions of the universe situated in one place — divided into many.
    Practical Applications
    • Cultivate the seeing of unity-in-multiplicity.
    • Don't choose between unity and diversity — both coexist in Him.
    • Use this paradox in your contemplation.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do I force-choose between unity and diversity?
    • What does both-at-once feel like?
    Analogy

    A traveller climbs to a vantage where, for the first time, every river he has ever crossed appears as a single map. They are still many rivers; they are still flowing; but now he sees them in one glance. So Arjuna sees the universe — divided into many, gathered in one.

    Stories
    Vyāsa Seeing the Whole

    Tradition holds that Vyāsa, before composing the Mahābhārata, beheld the entire course of events past, present, and future in a single act of yogic vision (Mahābhārata, Ādi-parva 1). Only because the totality had been seen in one place could it be narrated as one work.

    Arjuna's vision in 11.13 is briefer but of the same nature: eka-sthaṁ jagat kṛtsnam pravibhaktam anekadhā — one and divided at once. Such vision is what allows the seer to act inside time without being deceived by it.

    Important Words
    • vismaya - āviṣṭaḥ — overcome with wonder
      Compound: vismaya (wonder) + āviṣṭa (entered, possessed). Arjuna is not wondering — wonder has entered him. The grammar of devotional emotion is always passive.
    • hṛṣṭa - romā — hair standing on end
      One of the eight sāttvika-bhāvas in classical rasa-theory: romāñca, the involuntary bristling of body-hair in extreme emotion. The Gītā here records a textbook sāttvika sign.
    • praṇamya — having bowed
      Gerund of pra-nam. Sequential — first the bowing, then the speaking. Praise spoken from a standing posture is not the same praise.
    • śirasā — with the head
      Instrumental. Not a nod — the head itself goes to the ground. Body-language is theology in the Gītā's grammar.
    • kṛta - añjaliḥ — with folded hands
      Compound: kṛta (made) + añjali (the hollow of joined palms). The añjali is the universal Indic gesture of receiving — Arjuna's hands are formed to receive what is about to be spoken and seen.
    Then, bewildered and astonished, his hair standing on end, Arjuna bowed his head to offer obeisances and with folded hands began to pray to the Supreme Lord.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Sañjaya describes Arjuna's bodily response before any word: wonder, gooseflesh, bowed head, joined palms. The body marks the moment of darśana sacramentally before the mouth can compose a stotra.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The physiological signs (vismaya, hṛṣṭa-roma) are technical markers of sāttvika-bhāva in Sanskrit aesthetics — involuntary responses to overwhelming presence. The verse functions as a stage direction setting up the long Arjuna-stotra of 11.15-31. Hands and head, the two main organs of namaskāra, are both engaged.

    Purport

    Once the divine vision is revealed, the relationship between Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna changes immediately. Before, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna had a relationship based on friendship, but here, after the revelation, Arjuna is offering obeisances with great respect, and with folded hands he is praying to Kṛṣṇa. He is praising the universal form. Thus Arjuna’s relationship becomes one of wonder rather than friendship. Great devotees see Kṛṣṇa as the reservoir of all relationships. In the scriptures there are twelve basic kinds of relationships mentioned, and all of them are present in Kṛṣṇa. It is said that He is the ocean of all the relationships exchanged between two living entities, between the gods, or between the Supreme Lord and His devotees. Here Arjuna was inspired by the relationship of wonder, and in that wonder, although he was by nature very sober, calm and quiet, he became ecstatic, his hair stood up, and he began to offer his obeisances unto the Supreme Lord with folded hands. He was not, of course, afraid. He was affected by the wonders of the Supreme Lord. The immediate context is wonder; his natural loving friendship was overwhelmed by wonder, and thus he reacted in this way.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    14. Then, overcome with wonder, hair standing on end, Arjuna, bowing his head before the Lord and folding his hands in prayer, spoke.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    14. Then, overcome with wonder, hair standing on end, Arjuna, bowing his head before the Lord and folding his hands in prayer, spoke.
    Commentary

    Arjuna, who knew Kṛṣṇa, then experienced the rasa of adbhuta (astonishment) on seeing at that time the form with a thousand heads which he understood actually existed within Kṛṣṇa. Looking at Kṛṣṇa who had furnished this form, he spoke. Arjuna was the conqueror of all wealth (dhanaṁjayaḥ), and thus very steady, but with hairs standing on end, overcome with astonishment, after offering his respects to Kṛṣṇa by touching his head to the earth, he spoke with folded hands. It is hinted that he did not cover up his eyes out of fear, but displayed openly great astonishment. The Lord is the ālambana (the viṣaya) or object invoking rasa. [Note: This is part of vibhāva. In rasa there are five components: sattvika bhāva, anubhāva, saṣcari bhāva, vibhāva, and sthāyi bhāva. Vibhāva (preliminary factors) has two components: alambana (persons involved-viṣaya, object of love and āśraya, the experiencer) and uddīpana (stimulants).] When Arjuna looked at Him again and again, the gazing became the uddīpana, or instigation for rasa. Offering respects and folding hands are anubhāvas. Standing of hairs on end is the sāttvika bhāva. Mind overwhelmed by these elements, joy and steadiness are saṣcari bhāvas. By these four components, the fifth component, the sthāyī bhāva called viṣmaya became nourished, and the five together became adbhuta rasa.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Now Arjuna is seeing what previously he had heard about. He was astonished and bewildered but because he is a great ksatryia he didn't run away. But still, he put his head down in great astonishment and bewilderement. All the primary rasas and all, for except one, of the secondary rasas will be exhibited in this Chapter to Arjuna.

    Personal Guidance
    Bewildered with hairs standing on end, Arjuna bowed his head and offered prayers with folded hands.
    Practical Applications
    • Honor the body's response to spiritual reality (tears, hairs standing).
    • Don't suppress reverent body-response.
    • Pair body and prayer — bow physically when bowing internally.
    Reflection Questions
    • When did I last let my body fully respond to spiritual encounter?
    • What body-practice would honor those moments?
    Analogy

    When the temple doors finally open at the auspicious hour, the pilgrim does not declaim — he falls, hands joined, head down. Arjuna, the master archer, drops his stance and becomes a body of obeisance. The hair-on-end (hṛṣṭa-romā) is the body's own honest signal that the soul has met something larger.

    Stories
    Akrūra in the Yamunā

    When Akrūra was driving Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to Mathurā (SB 10.39), he stepped into the Yamunā to bathe and there beheld the four-armed form of Viṣṇu with conch, disc, mace, and lotus, attended by all the great sages. His hair stood on end, tears poured forth, and he could only fold his hands and pray.

    Arjuna's response in 11.14 is identical: praṇamya śirasā kṛta-añjaliḥ. Different devotees, different settings — same bodily grammar of darśana.

    Important Words

      First-person singular present — the verse's signature verb. Arjuna will repeat it through verses 15–19 like a refrain; the granted divya-cakṣus is now active in real time.
    • devān — the demigods
      Accusative plural. The devas are objects of perception inside Kṛṣṇa — not separate gods to be appeased, but functions of the one Lord.
    • brahmāṇam — Brahmā
      Accusative. Even the highest cosmic functionary, the four-headed creator, appears inside the form — placing Kṛṣṇa above the entire trimūrti hierarchy.
    • kamala - āsana - stham — seated on the lotus
      Compound: lotus + seat + standing. The classical iconography of Brahmā is preserved exactly — Arjuna sees him in his canonical posture, sitting on the navel-lotus from Viṣṇu (cf. SB 3.8).
    • uragān — the serpents
      Lit. 'breast-going,' those that move by the chest. Even the serpentine race — Ananta, Vāsuki — is included. Nothing is left outside the form.
    • divyān — divine
      Adjective. Sañjaya keeps marking 'divine' to insist that what Arjuna sees is not mythic invention but real spiritual category.
    Arjuna said: My dear Lord Kṛṣṇa, I see assembled in Your body all the demigods and various other living entities. I see Brahmā sitting on the lotus flower, as well as Lord Śiva and all the sages and divine serpents.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Arjuna's stotra opens with a survey: the gods, every class of being, Brahmā on the lotus, ṛṣis, divine nāgas — all inside the one body. He begins not with terror but with sheer inventory, as if naming each item helps him hold the vision.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The metre shifts to Triṣṭubh (Upajāti) for 11.15-50, signaling a high-style hymnic register. Brahmā 'kamala-āsana-stha' is the demiurge born from Viṣṇu's navel-lotus (Bhāgavata 3.8); seeing Brahmā inside Kṛṣṇa establishes the hierarchy that ch. 10 had asserted ('ahaṁ ādir hi devānāṁ', 10.2). The catalog mirrors but exceeds 11.6 because Arjuna now sees, not just hears.

    Purport

    Arjuna sees everything in the universe; therefore he sees Brahmā, who is the first creature in the universe, and the celestial serpent upon which the Garbhodaka-śāyī Viṣṇu lies in the lower regions of the universe. This snake bed is called Vāsuki. There are also other snakes known as Vāsuki. Arjuna can see from the Garbhodaka-śāyī Viṣṇu up to the topmost part of the universe on the lotus-flower planet where Brahmā, the first creature of the universe, resides. That means that from the beginning to the end, everything could be seen by Arjuna, who was sitting in one place on his chariot. This was possible by the grace of the Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    15. Arjuna said: In Your body I see all the devatās, as well as the mass of all the beings. I see Lord Brahmā, seated on a lotus, all the ṛṣis, and shining snakes.
    Commentary

    I see a multitude of viviparous animals (bhūtā-viśeṣa) and Brahmā situated on Mount Meru at the center of the lotus of the earth planet.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    15. Arjuna said: In Your body I see all the devatās, as well as the mass of all the beings. I see Lord Brahma, Viṣṇu, who is situated within Brahmā sitting on his lotus, all the ṛṣis, and shining snakes.
    Commentary

    What did he say? This is described in seven verses. I see a collection of creatures born from wombs (bhūta viśeṣa), as well as Brahmā with four heads, and Viṣṇu situated as antaryāmin within the lotus-seated Brahmā (kamalāsana stham), who is Garbhodakaśayi Viṣṇu (iśam). I see snakes such as Vāsuki (uragān).

    Theme

    COMMON THEME: Arjuna speaks ‘his realisations’ of the Universal Form

    PLEASE NOTE: All points of the purports are included as the sub-points; as such there are no individual ‘Focus of

    Learning’ sections for these verses.

    ARJUNA’S DESCRIPTION OF THE UNIVERSAL FORM

    All living entities at one place – See’s all demigods and living entities assembled in that form – Lord Brahma sitting on a lotus flower, also Lord Siva and all the sages and divine serpents (11.15)
    To see all at one place is possible only by Krishna’s grace
    Krishna is unlimited – See’s many many arms, bellies, mouths, eyes without any limit and with no end, middle and beginning (11.16)
    Through Him, everything could be seen
    Blazing like sun (11.17) –
    Analogy: Glaring effulgence on all sides like a blazing fire or immeasurable radiance like the sun
    This form is very difficult to see
    Arjuna attempts to describe immeasurable – He is trying to say “You are the Supreme Lord” by the following statements: (11.18*)
    You are the Supreme primal objective
    Ultimate resting place of all the universe
    Inexhaustible / oldest
    Maintainer of eternal religion
    Sun and moon are your eyes (11.19)

    Personal Guidance
    Arjuna says: I see all the demigods within Your body, including Brahmā on the lotus, all the sages, the celestial serpents.
    Practical Applications
    • Recognize the Vedic cosmology as actually present within Kṛṣṇa.
    • Don't treat 'demigods' as defunct mythology.
    • Honor the cosmic furniture of devotion.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I dismissed Vedic cosmology as outdated?
    • What does taking it seriously open?
    Analogy

    A scholar opens what he thought was a chapter and finds it is the whole library — every author, every sage, every god he has ever heard of, gathered between two covers. Arjuna opens the form of Kṛṣṇa and finds the entire pantheon inside.

    Stories
    Aśvatthāmā Confronted with Nārāyaṇa

    After his crimes at the close of the war, Aśvatthāmā released the brahmāstra and Arjuna countered (Mahābhārata, Sauptika-parva 13–16). Vyāsa appeared between the two weapons. Aśvatthāmā then perceived Kṛṣṇa as the source of all the demigods he had invoked — he saw on Kṛṣṇa's chest the whole array of devas and ṛṣis.

    Arjuna's vision in 11.15 is the same recognition: every devatā he has ever worshiped is inside the one form. The Gītā is firm — the demigods are real, and they are in Kṛṣṇa.

    Important Words
    • aneka — many
      Again the chapter's pressure-word. Arjuna repeats it; words that do not exhaust the count must at least register the failure to count.
    • ananta - rūpam — of unlimited form
      Compound: an-anta (without end) + rūpa (form). A form that paradoxically has no boundary — the verse's central contradiction-as-truth.
    • na antam — no end
      Negation + accusative. Antaḥ means end; here it is denied. The Gauḍīya reading is positive: an-anta is a name of the Lord Himself — Ananta-śeṣa, on whom Viṣṇu reclines. Arjuna is not negating predicates; he is seeing unlimitedness as Bhagavān's own personal attribute.
    • na madhyam — no middle
      The middle is the test of finitude — a thing with a middle has two ends. Denying the middle denies the framework that would let one locate beginning and end.
    • viśva - īśvara — O Lord of the universe
      Vocative compound. The same form Arjuna cannot measure is the īśvara of the entire viśva. Limitlessness and lordship are one fact.
    • viśva - rūpa — O universal form
      Vocative compound. The proper name of this chapter's vision. Arjuna at last calls Kṛṣṇa by this title — and the title will stay attached to this manifestation in tradition forever.
    O Lord of the universe, O universal form, I see in Your body many, many arms, bellies, mouths and eyes, expanded everywhere, without limit. I see in You no end, no middle and no beginning.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण
    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.
    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    From inventory Arjuna moves to limit: he can find none. Anywhere he looks, more form. Beginning, middle, end — the standard frame of any object — fail to fit. The vocative 'viśva-rūpa' enters the Gītā here as a name for what cannot be circumscribed.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Negation triplet 'na antaṁ na madhyaṁ na ādim' parallels the Upaniṣadic 'anādi-madhya-anta' negations (cf. 11.19 below; Śvetāśvatara 6.9). The word 'viśva-rūpa' is doctrinally loaded — it names this whole chapter (Viśvarūpa-darśana-yoga) and the form that will be withdrawn in 11.50 to relieve Arjuna's terror.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    16. I see You everywhere with infinite form, with many arms, stomachs, mouths and eyes. O lord of the universe, origin of all this! O form of the universe! I do not see a beginning, middle or end of this form of Yours.
    Commentary

    Arjuna then describes the forms of devas and others that he saw in the body of the universal form. O form of the universe! This means the first puruṣa (mahā viṣṇu).

    11.16 अनेकबाहूदरवक्त्रनेत्रम् with manifold arms? stomachs? mouths and eyes? पश्यामि (I) see? त्वाम् Thee? सर्वतः on every side? अनन्तरूपम् of boundless form? न not? अनत्म् end? न not? मध्यम् middle? न not? पुनः,again? तव Thy? आदिम् origin? पश्यामि (I) see? विश्वेश्वर O Lord of the universe? विश्वरूप O Cosmic Form.Commentary A thing that is limited by space and time has a begining? a middle and an end? but the Lord is omnipresent and eternal.     Personal Guidance
    I see Your unlimited expansions — many arms, bellies, mouths, eyes — without beginning, middle, or end.
    Practical Applications
    • Hold the numerical immensity Kṛṣṇa is showing.
    • Don't shrink-fit Kṛṣṇa to fit your imagination.
    • Cultivate awe rather than mastery.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I been trying to master what only awes?
    • What does awe restore?
    Analogy

    The map of a coastline can be drawn from one side; the map of a sphere cannot. Wherever you start, the sphere has no edge. Arjuna's mind, trained on coastline-things, now meets a sphere — and the words 'no end, no middle, no beginning' are the only honest geometry.

    Stories
    The Beggar Brāhmaṇa in the Bhāgavatam

    In the eleventh canto (SB 11.7–8), Lord Kṛṣṇa narrates the story of the avadhūta brāhmaṇa who had twenty-four gurus drawn from nature. From the sky as guru he learned that the Lord, though pervading all bodies, is without beginning, middle, or end — anantam — and remains untouched by what He pervades.

    Arjuna's words in 11.16 are this same teaching seen rather than heard. The sky has no edge; the form he beholds has no edge; the parallel is exact.

    Important Words
    • kirīṭinam — with crowns
      Accusative of kirīṭin, 'crown-bearer.' The crown identifies the cosmic king, and 'crowns' in the plural acknowledges that He bears them across all His manifestations.
    • gadinam — with maces
      Accusative of gadin. The gadā Kaumodakī is Viṣṇu's signature weapon. Arjuna sees it on this terrible form, anchoring the universal vision to the familiar four-armed iconography.
    • cakriṇam — with discs
      Accusative of cakrin. The Sudarśana-cakra — the wheel that protects devotees and severs ego. Its presence here promises that the awful vision is still Kṛṣṇa's, still wielding the same protective wheel.
    • tejaḥ - rāśim — mass of effulgence
      Compound: tejas (radiant energy) + rāśi (heap, accumulation). Not light scattered; light heaped. The accumulation is itself the form's substance.
    • durnirīkṣyam — difficult to see
      Compound: duḥ (hard) + nir-īkṣ (to gaze). Even with divya-cakṣus, the gazing is difficult. The eye is enabled, not made omnipotent.
    • aprameyam — immeasurable
      From a-pra-mā, 'not able to be measured.' One of the Lord's standard epithets in the Upaniṣads. Measurement presupposes a measure — there is none here.
    Your form is difficult to see because of its glaring effulgence, spreading on all sides, like blazing fire or the immeasurable radiance of the sun. Yet I see this glowing form everywhere, adorned with various crowns, clubs and discs.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण
    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.
    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    The Viṣṇu-iconography (crown, mace, discus) appears inside the cosmic blaze, identifying the universal form as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa Himself. Yet it is 'durnirīkṣya' — too bright to look at — preparing the shift in Arjuna's tone from delight to dread.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The verse threads two registers: the recognizable Viṣṇu icons (kirīṭa, gadā, cakra) and the unbounded fire-light. This anchors the vision: even at maximum cosmic scale, the Lord remains the same Viṣṇu of Vaikuṇṭha. 'Durnirīkṣya' is the first real hint that this gift is hard to bear; 11.24 develops it into pravyathita.

    Translation
    17. I see You with crown, club, cakra, a mass of light shining everywhere, difficult to behold, with immeasurable radiance on all sides like the blazing of fire and sun.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    17. I see You with crown, club, cakra, a mass of light shining everywhere, difficult to behold, with immeasurable radiance on all sides like the blazing of fire and sun.
    Commentary

    Now he describes that form in another way. Thought difficult to behold, I can see You, because by Your mercy I have attained celestial eyes. The form is difficult to behold because on all sides it is as brilliant as blazing fire. Thus it is impossible to measure it (aprameyam).

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    It is immeasurable, but it has some specific elements that we should note what this universal form is: (1) it is immeasurable, (2) it has a great, great radiance, (3) everything is situated in one place (all the universes, the demigods, etc..., everything in one place). These are, at this point, the main qualities of the universal form. Now in next verse Arjuna is going to try to describe the immeasurable.

    Personal Guidance
    I see You wearing crowns, holding clubs and discs, brilliant beyond measure — like blazing fire, the immeasurable sun, dazzling.
    Practical Applications
    • Honor Kṛṣṇa's regal, weapon-bearing, blazing aspect.
    • Don't sentimentalize Him into only sweetness.
    • Recognize majesty as part of His full identity.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I sentimentalized away His majesty?
    • What does restored majesty add?
    Analogy

    Looking directly at a welder's arc burns the eye even though the arc is small; the radiance is not measured by size. Arjuna is now looking at the welder's arc of the cosmos — durnirīkṣyam, hard to look upon — and the only way he can describe it is by what it resembles, blazing fire and the sun.

    Stories
    Bhīṣma's Vision on the Bed of Arrows

    Lying on his bed of arrows, the dying Bhīṣma beheld Kṛṣṇa with his last sight and offered the Bhīṣma-stuti (SB 1.9.32–42). He saw Kṛṣṇa as 'the supreme effulgence' (paraṁ jyotiḥ) shining like the sun upon all directions — kirīṭinaṁ kuṇḍalinam, crowned and bejewelled, with weapons at the ready.

    The iconographic vocabulary of BG 11.17 — crowned, with mace and disc, blazing like fire and the sun — is the same Bhīṣma uses. Two warriors, two darśanas, identical witness.

    Important Words
    • akṣaram — imperishable
      From a-kṣar, 'that which does not flow away.' One of the Gītā's deepest titles for the Lord (cf. 8.3, 8.11, 15.16–18). Arjuna names Kṛṣṇa as akṣara before the chapter's most terrible verses arrive, anchoring himself in the imperishable as the perishable rushes by.
    • veditavyam — to be known
      Future passive participle of vid — 'that which ought to be known.' The form is not just seen but to-be-known; sight is the doorway, knowledge is the room.
    • nidhānam — resting place
      From ni-dhā, 'to lay down.' The Lord is the storehouse, the deposit-place of the universe. When the universe withdraws, it withdraws into Him.
    • śāśvata - dharma - goptā — maintainer of the eternal religion
      Compound: śāśvata (eternal) + dharma (religion) + goptā (protector). Kṛṣṇa is named in His function from BG 4.7–8: He descends to protect dharma. Arjuna recognises this function in the form before him.
    • sanātanaḥ — eternal
      Adjective from sa-nā, 'always existing.' The same root behind sanātana-dharma. Arjuna calls the Lord by the very word that names the eternal way.
    • puruṣaḥ — the Personality
      Person, not impersonal essence. Even at the moment of beholding the all-pervading form, Arjuna's word is puruṣa. The Gītā's personalist commitment is preserved at the chapter's most cosmic moment.
    You are the supreme primal objective. You are the ultimate resting place of all this universe. You are inexhaustible, and You are the oldest. You are the maintainer of the eternal religion, the Personality of Godhead. This is my opinion.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Arjuna inserts a doctrinal credo into the stotra: the form before him is the Upaniṣadic akṣara-puruṣa, the world's support, the protector of sanātana-dharma. Vision is fast becoming theology — 'mato me' (in my opinion) signs his personal acceptance.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Four titles in series: parama akṣara (cf. Muṇḍaka 1.1.6), paraṁ nidhāna (resting-place, cf. 9.18), śāśvata-dharma-goptā (guardian of eternal Dharma, recalling 4.7-8's avatāra-vow), sanātana puruṣa (the ancient Person, Puruṣa-sūkta 'puruṣa evedaṁ sarvam'). The verse compresses the Upaniṣadic vocabulary and aligns it with Kṛṣṇa-identity.

    Translation
    18. You are known as the supreme Brahman. You are the place of destruction of this universe. You are indestructible, the protector of eternal dharma. I know that You are the eternal person.
    Commentary

    You are known by the strivers for liberation as Brahman (akṣaram). You are the place of destruction of all things (nidhānam).

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    18. You are known as the supreme brahman. You are the shelter of everything. You are indestructible, the protector of eternal dharma. I know that You are the ancient person.
    Commentary

    Seeing this inconceivable great power, I am convinced about You. That is the purport of this verse. You are to be known (veditavyam). This is described by statements of the Vedas such as atha parā yayā tad akṣaram adhigamyate, yat tad adṛśyam: the higher knowledge is that by which the indestructible Brahman is apprehended, which cannot be seen. (Muṇḍaka Upanisad 1.1.5) Described in the Vedas, You are known as the truth with all opulences (paramam akṣaram). You are the shelter (nidhānam). You are the indestructible (avyayaḥ). You are the protector of dharma spoken in the Vedas (śāśvata dharma goptā). You alone are the ancient person (sanātanaḥ puruṣaḥ), mentioned in the mantra sa kāraṇaṁ kāraṇādhipādhipo na cāsya kaścij janitā na cādhipaḥ: He is the cause, master of the senses; He has no lord or creator. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.9)

    ARJUNA’S DESCRIPTION OF THE UNIVERSAL FORM

    All living entities at one place – See’s all demigods and living entities assembled in that form – Lord Brahma sitting on a lotus flower, also Lord Siva and all the sages and divine serpents (11.15)
    To see all at one place is possible only by Krishna’s grace
    Krishna is unlimited – See’s many many arms, bellies, mouths, eyes without any limit and with no end, middle and beginning (11.16)
    Through Him, everything could be seen
    Blazing like sun (11.17) –
    Analogy: Glaring effulgence on all sides like a blazing fire or immeasurable radiance like the sun
    This form is very difficult to see
    Arjuna attempts to describe immeasurable – He is trying to say “You are the Supreme Lord” by the following statements: (11.18*)
    You are the Supreme primal objective
    Ultimate resting place of all the universe
    Inexhaustible / oldest
    Maintainer of eternal religion
    Sun and moon are your eyes (11.19)
    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.18 Tvam, You; are the aksaram, Immutable; the paramam, supreme One, Brahman; veditavyam, to be known-by those aspiring for Liberation. You are the param, most perfect; nidhanam, repository-where things are deposited, i.e. the ultimate resort; asya visvasya, of this Universe, of the entire creation. Further. You are the avyayah, Imperishable-there is no decay in You; the sasvata-dharma-gopta, Protector (gopta) of the ever-existing (sasvata) religion (dharma). You are the sanatanah, eternal; transcendental purusah, Person. This is me, my; matah, belief-what is meant by me. Moreover,
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.18 You alone are the Supreme 'Imperishable Person' indicated as that which ought to be realised in such Upanisadic passages as: 'Two sciences are to be known' (Mun. U., 1.1.4). You alone are the 'Supreme Substratum' of the universe, i.e., supreme support of this universe. You are 'immutable', namely, not liable to mutation. Whatever might be your attributes and divine manifestations, You remain unchanged in Your form. You alone are the guardian of 'the eternal law' - You who protect the eternal Dharma of the Veda by incarnations like this. I know you are the everlasting Person. I know You are the eternal Person, described in such passages as, 'I know this great Purusa' (Tai. A., 3.12.7) and 'Person who is higher than the high' (Mun. U., 3.2.8). You, who were till now known to me as the most distinguished of the race of Yadu, have been realised by me now through direct perception as of this nature, i.e., of a nature unknown to me before. Such is the meaning.
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical
    Translation
    11.18 Tvam aksaram etc. Guardian of the pious acts of the Satvatas. Satvatas are the same as the Satvatas i.e. those who are established in the Truth that does not take cognizance of any difference between the Action (11.Spanda) and the Consciousness; the Truth which is nothing but Existentiality and is in the form of Awarenes. Their pious act is that act [of meditation] of theirs which - on account of its being continously engaged in the process of undertaking and rejecting [things] - consists of the act of emanation and absorption, and is the most superior of all the paths [leading to salvation]. The Lord protects that pious act. This is the secret in this chapter and it has been made almost clear by me (11.Ag.) in my (11.Ag.'s) Vivrti (11.Commentary) on the Devistotra (11.Goddess-Hymn). That is self-evident to the learned readers, with critical accuman, and initiation. Hence, why to take recourse to the verbiage of explaining again and again what is already known very clearly.
    Swami Sivananda Classical
    Translation
    11.18 Thou art the Imperishable, the Supreme Being, worthy to be known. Thou art the great treasure-house of this universe; Thou art the imperishable protector of the eternal Dhrama; Thou art the Primal Person, I deem.
    Commentary

    11.18 त्वम् Thou? अक्षरम् imperishable? परमम् the Supreme Being? वेदितव्यम् worthy to be known? त्वम् Thou? अस्य (of) this? विश्वस्य of universe? परम् the great? निधानम् treasurehouse? त्वम् Thou? अव्ययः imperishable? शाश्वतधर्मगोप्ता Protector of the Eternal Dharma? सनातनः ancient? त्वम् Thou? पुरुषः Purusha? मतः thought? मे of me.Commentary VisvasyaNidhaanam Treasurehouse of this universe? also means abode or refuge or the substratum of this universe. It is because of this that all the beings in the universe are preserved and protected. He is the inexhaustibel source to Whom the devotee turns at all times. Deluded indeed are they that ignore this divine treasurehouse and runa fter the shadow of the objects of the senses which do not contain even an iota of pleasure.Veditavyam To be known by the aspirants or seekrs of liberation? through Sravana (hearing of the scriptures)? Manana (reflection) and Nididhyasana (meditation).Avyayah means inexhaustible? unchanging? undying.

    Personal Guidance
    You are the supreme original goal, the ultimate resting place, the eternal protector of religion — the imperishable Supreme.
    Practical Applications
    • Use these epithets in daily prayer.
    • Don't reduce Kṛṣṇa to one role; hold the breadth.
    • Read this verse aloud during dark periods.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which epithet most steadies me when I'm shaky?
    • Why?
    Analogy

    When a builder shows you the foundation, the walls, and the roof of his house, he is showing you a house — finite and time-bound. When the Lord shows Himself, He must be both the foundation and the architect and the dweller all at once. Arjuna names Him as that complete reality.

    Stories
    Brahmā's Realisation in the Catuḥ-ślokī

    Brahmā, after long austerity, received from the Lord four foundational verses (SB 2.9.32–35): the Lord alone existed before, exists now, and will exist after; the Lord is the imperishable ground of everything. Brahmā then composed the Brahma-saṁhitā around this realisation, opening with īśvaraḥ paramaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ.

    Arjuna's words in 11.18 — tvam akṣaraṁ paramaṁ veditavyam — are this same conclusion. Brahmā arrived by tapas; Arjuna by darśana; the destination is identical.

    Important Words
    • anādi — without beginning
      Compound: an (not) + ādi (beginning). One of the Gītā's most loaded words (cf. 13.13, 15.3). Without beginning means uncreated, self-existent — the Lord is not anyone's effect.
    • ananta — unlimited
      Compound: an + anta (end). Used here both for vīryam (power) and bāhum (arms). Arjuna applies the word to two different attributes in one verse; the Lord's limitlessness is multi-dimensional.
    • vīryam — potency
      From vīra, 'hero.' Heroic power, the vital energy of action. The Lord's vīrya is what carries out cosmic functions — creating, sustaining, destroying.
    • śaśi — moon
      Nominative. The moon, named alongside the sun in the same verse — together they form the dual eyes of the cosmic body. The Puruṣa-sūkta is in the background.
    • sūrya — sun
      Nominative. Paired with śaśi as the second of the two cosmic eyes. The luminaries are not symbols; in this vision they are organs of one body.
    • hutāśa - vaktram — fire-eating mouth
      Compound: huta-āśa (eater of oblations, i.e. Agni) + vaktra (mouth). Foreshadows the devouring vision of verses 25–30 — the same mouth that eats oblations will be seen eating warriors.
    You are without origin, middle or end. Your glory is unlimited. You have numberless arms, and the sun and moon are Your eyes. I see You with blazing fire coming forth from Your mouth, burning this entire universe by Your own radiance.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Three 'ananta' epithets pile up — no boundary in time, in power, in limbs. The cosmos is being burned by the very brilliance of the one in whom it stands. The benevolent vibhūti-survey of ch. 10 is now seen with its scorching edge.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    'Śaśi-sūrya-netram' (moon-and-sun-eyed) is a Vedic trope (cf. Puruṣa-sūkta: 'candramā manaso jātaḥ, cakṣoḥ sūryo ajāyata'). Here the cosmic body has the luminaries as eyes, reversing the cause-effect chain. 'Sva-tejasā viśvam tapantam' prepares the imminent shift into the kāla-rūpa: the same heat that sustains can also consume.

    Purport

    There is no limit to the extent of the six opulences of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Here and in many other places there is repetition, but according to the scriptures, repetition of the glories of Kṛṣṇa is not a literary weakness. It is said that at a time of bewilderment or wonder or of great ecstasy, statements are repeated over and over. That is not a flaw.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    19. I see You are without beginning, middle or end, possessed of infinite strength, infinite arms, with the sun and moon for Your eyes, with a mouth of blazing fire, burning this universe with its heat.
    Commentary

    With words like anādi, Arjuna seems to repeat himself. Do not find fault however with the repetition in the words of Arjuna, who was submerged in the ocean of the rasa of great astonishment (mahā-viṣmaya-rasa). It is said: prasāde viṣmaye harṣe dvi-trir-uktaṁ na duṣyati: repetition of statements two or three times due to joy, astonishment or kindness is not a fault.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    19. I see You are without beginning, middle or end, possessed of infinite strength, a thousand arms, with the sun and moon for Your eyes, with a mouth of blazing fire, burning this universe with Your heat.
    Commentary

    I see You without beginning, middle or end. You have infinite vīrya or potency. This infers all the six opulences: vīrya, yaśas, śrī, jṣāna, vairāgya and aiśvarya. [Note: Another list of the six is: jṇāna, śakti, vairāgya, aiśvarya, vīrya and tejaḥ.] You have thousands of arms (ananta bāahum), and eyes like the sun and moon. Your eyes are pleasing (like the moon) to the devas who are obedient to You, and harsh (like the sun) to the demons who disobey You. Your mouths are like a blazing fire, similar to the fire of destruction. Repetition of items in Arjuna’s words is not a fault, as he was overcome with astonishment. It is said prasāde vismaye harṣe dvi-trir-uktaṁ na duṣyati: uttering statements two or three times out of joy, dismay or kindness is not a fault.

    Now Arjuna describes Kala-rupa

    COMMON THEME: Text 11.19 marks the beginning of description of ‘Kala-rupa’ (The form as Time) which

    continues up till Text 11.31

    

    

    ARJUNA’S FURTHER DESCRIPTION OF THE UNIVERSAL FORM AS ‘KALA-RUPA’.

    Blazing fire coming forth from your mouth, burning this entire universe (11.19)
    Numberless arms and sun and moon are the eyes
    Without origin, middle and end
    Repetition of glories is not a flaw – It is a sign of bewilderment, wonder or great ecstasy
    Spread throughout – Spread throughout the sky and planets and all space in between; and all the planetary systems are perturbed seeing you (11.20)
    ‘Dyav-a-prthivyoh’ (Space between heaven and earth) and ‘Loka-trayam’ (Three worlds) –indicate that not only Arjuna saw, but other planetary systems, whoever endowed with divine vision, also saw this form and got perturbed
    This proves that Arjuna’s seeing was not a dream
    Petitioned by demigods – Kala-rupa is petitioned by demigods and sages – All are fearful (11.21 – 11.22)
    Demigods are surrendering and praying with folded hands
    Great sages are praying with Vedic hymns
    Siva, Adityas, Vasus etc beholding You in wonder
    Rasa changes to fear – Arjuna experiences a terrible fearsome sight (11.23)
    Arjuna loses steadiness and equilibrium of mind, because mind is perturbed by fear (11.24)
    Arjuna sees blazing death-like faces and awful teeth (11.25)
    Link between texts 11.25 & 11.26: Text 11.26 through 11.30 describe future occurrences that Arjuna sees within the kala-rupa. In Text 11.7, Krishna said that Arjuna could see “whatever *he+ may want to see in the future.” In these texts, Arjuna sees that Bhisma, Drona and Karna – the three most feared members of the opposing army – will be destroyed.
    Two Analogies: Devouring all soldiers of both armies on both sides, including Bhisma, Drona & Karna, rushing into Your mouth (11.26 – 11.27)
    Analogy: As many waves of river flow into the ocean (11.28)
    Analogy: As moths dash to destruction in blazing fire (11.29*)
    Indicates that Arjuna could see his awaited victory
    All-devouring – You are devouring all people from all sides, your effulgence is covering all the universe with terrible scorching rays(11.30)

    ARJUNA’S QUESTIONS

    Arjuna in great fear asks two questions (11.31)
    Who are You?
    What is Your mission?
    Why Arjuna asks these questions – Because although Arjuna knew Krishna as his friend and Supreme Personality of Godhead, but he was puzzled by various forms exhibited by Krishna
    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.19 Pasyami, I see; tvam, You; as anadi-madhya-antam, without beginning, middle and end; ananta-viryam, possessed of infinite valour; and also ananta-bahum, having innumerable arms; sasi-surya-netram, having the sun and the moon as the eyes; dipta-hutasavakram, having a mouth like a blazing fire; tapantam, heating up; idam, this; visvam, Universe; sva-tejasa, by Your own birlliance.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.19 I behold You as without beginning, middle and end. Your might is infinite, of unsurpassed excellence. Here the term 'might' is used for illustration. The meaning is that You are the sole repository of knowledge, strength, sovereignty, valour, power and glory, one whose excellence cannot be surpassed. Your arms are infinite, i.e., they are countless. This is also for illustration, implying that You have an infinite number of arms, stomachs, feet, mouths etc. The sun and moon are Your eyes; all Your eyes are like the moon and the sun, beaming with grace and power. The grace is directed towards the devotees like the gods who offer salutations etc., and power is directed against Asuras, Raksasas etc., who are opposed to these. For it will be said later on: 'The Raksasas flee on all sides in fear, and all the hosts of Siddhas bow down to You' (11.36). Your mouth is emitting fire, namely, the fire appropriate for destroying all things, as the Fire of Time consumes the world at the time of dissolution. With Your own radiance You are warming the universe. By radiance (Tejas) is meant the poweer to vanish others. I behold You warming (or governing) the universe with Your own radiance. The meaning is this: 'I directly realise You' as taught before as the Creator of all, as the supporter of everything, as the sovereign over everything, as the destroyer of everything, as the ocean of knowledge and other infinite attributes, as without beginning, middle and end, and as possessing a divine body of this nature. How, in one divine body, can there be many stomachs etc.? This is possible in the following way: From a hip of infinite extent, stomachs etc., as described, branc off upwards. The divine feet etc., branch off downwards. So there is no contradiction in attributing a pair of eyes for each face. 'On perceiving You to be thus, the gods etc., and myself, have become frightened - says Arjuna in the following words:
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical
    Translation
    11.19 Sri Abhinavagupta did not comment upon this sloka.
    Swami Sivananda Classical
    Translation
    11.19 I see Thee without beginning, middle or end, infinite in power, of endless arms, the sun and the moon being Thy eyes, the burning fire Thy mouth, heating the whole universe with Thy radiance.
    Commentary

    11.19 अनादिमध्यान्तम् without beginning? middle or end? अनन्तवीर्यम् infinite in power? अनन्तबाहुम् of endless arms? शशिसूर्यनेत्रम् Thy eyes as the sun and the moon? पश्यामि (I) see? त्वाम् Thee? दीप्तहुताशवक्त्रम् Thy mouth as the burning fire? स्वतेजसा with Thy radiance? विश्वम् the universe? इदम् this? तपन्तम् heating.Commentary Anantabahu Having endless arms. This denotes that the multiplicity of His limbs are endless.

    Swami Gambhīrānanda Classical
    Translation
    11.19 I see You as without beginning, middle and end, possessed of infinite valour, having innumerable arms, having the sun and the moon as eyes, having a mouth like a blazing fire, and heating up this Universe by Your own brilliance.
    Shri Purohit Swami Classical

    11.19 Without beginning, without middle and without end, infinite in power, Thine arms all-embracing, the sun and moon Thine eyes, Thy face beaming with the fire of sacrifice, flooding the whole universe with light.

    Personal Guidance
    You are without origin, middle, or end — Your power unlimited, Your arms innumerable; sun and moon are Your eyes.
    Practical Applications
    • Hold cosmic scale in your imagination of Kṛṣṇa.
    • Use sun and moon as eyes-of-the-Lord meditation.
    • Don't reduce Kṛṣṇa to local.
    Reflection Questions
    • When did I last connect with sun or moon as His eye?
    • What does that practice offer?
    Analogy

    Imagine a single sentence in which every word is the first word and the last word and the middle — that is the shape of what Arjuna is trying to describe. Without origin, middle, or end, the sun and moon must serve as eyes because there is no larger body to host them.

    Stories
    The Puruṣa-sūkta

    The Ṛg-veda's Puruṣa-sūkta (10.90) describes the cosmic Person from whose mouth came the Brāhmaṇas, from whose arms the Kṣatriyas, from whose eyes the sun, from whose mind the moon. The hymn predates the Gītā by centuries and is the canonical Vedic background of this very verse.

    When Arjuna says śaśi-sūrya-netram — moon-and-sun-eyed — he is echoing the Puruṣa-sūkta with his own eyes. The vision and the hymn are not two things; the hymn was always a description of what Arjuna is now seeing.

    Important Words
    • dyau — heaven
      Nominative of div, the upper world. With ā-pṛthivyoḥ, the verse spans the Vedic cosmos top to bottom — heaven and earth as the two poles, the Lord filling between.
    • vyāptam — pervaded
      Past passive participle of vi-āp, 'to fill out completely.' Not occupied, not visited — pervaded, every space already saturated.
    • ekena — by one
      Instrumental singular. The pervasion is accomplished by one being, not by many. Monotheism's grammar in a single word.
    • ugram — terrible
      Adjective. The first time in the chapter Arjuna calls the form ugra — fierce, dreadful. The descriptive register is about to shift toward fear.
    • loka — the worlds
      Plural in compound (loka-trayam). The classical three worlds — bhūr, bhuvar, svar. All three are pravyathita, shaking.
    • pravyathitam — perturbed
      Past participle of pra-vyath, 'to tremble in distress.' The verb will be repeated in 11.23 (lokāḥ pravyathitāḥ) and 11.24 (antar-ātmā pravyathita) — Arjuna marks the trembling at three concentric levels: form, worlds, his own self.
    Although You are one, You spread throughout the sky and the planets and all space between. O great one, seeing this wondrous and terrible form, all the planetary systems are perturbed.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण
    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.
    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    The vision now widens beyond Arjuna: he reports that the three worlds themselves are quaking. The form is adbhuta (wondrous) and ugra (fierce) in one stroke — beauty and terror in the same object. 'Tvayā ekena' — by You alone — is the monotheistic kernel.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    'Loka-trayaṁ pravyathitam' anticipates 11.23 where Arjuna himself joins that pravyathita state. The word ugra ('fierce') now openly enters; from this verse to 11.31 the dominant register is bhayānaka-rasa. The pādas echo the Puruṣa-sūkta image of a Person filling space.

    he mahā-ātman! dyau-ā-pṛthivyoḥ idam antaraṃ sarvāḥ diśaḥ ca tvayā ekena hi vyāptam; tava idam adbhutam ugraṃ rūpaṃ dṛṣṭvā loka-trayaṃ pravyathitam |
    O great Self, this entire space between heaven and earth, and all the directions, are pervaded by You alone; seeing this wondrous, fierce form of Yours, the three worlds are agitated.

    Purport

    Dyāv ā-pṛthivyoḥ (“the space between heaven and earth”) and loka-trayam (“the three worlds”) are significant words in this verse because it appears that not only did Arjuna see this universal form of the Lord, but others in other planetary systems saw it also. Arjuna’s seeing of the universal form was not a dream. All whom the Lord endowed with divine vision saw that universal form on the battlefield.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    20. The space between heaven and earth and all directions are filled with You alone. Seeing this astonishing and ferocious form of Yours, the three worlds have become terrified, O great soul.
    Commentary

    Now that Arjuna had the proper qualification, the Lord shows him His form as time. This is described in ten verses.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    20. The space between heaven and earth and all directions are filled with You alone. Seeing this astonishing and ferocious form of Yours, the three worlds have become terrified, O great soul.
    Commentary

    In ten verses the Lord shows His form as time, after Arjuna had attained fitness in disposition for seeing that form. The space between heaven and earth and all directions are pervaded by You alone, one form. Seeing this ferocious, astounding and unlimited form of Yours, the three worlds are agitated and fearful (pravyathitam). O shelter of all (mahātman-great soul, covering the three worlds)! It is understood that now, for seeing the war, the devas, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras and others who were friendly or neutral had gathered. Not only Arjuna was given celestial eyes. They also were given celestial eyes by the Lord to see this form. If only Arjuna could see that form, it would have been like a sleeping person seeing chariots or other objects in a dream, while others could not see them. The Lord did this so that many others could bear witness His powers.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Now Arjuna is going to describe another element ‑ the disturbing element. There was 'everything situated in one place with a great effulgence', now another element is entering in ‑ it is called Krsna's 'kala rupa', or form of time which Krsna has already sais "it is the destructive element". Krsna, out of His mercy, is giving also the vision of His universal form to the demigods. They all have come to see it, they are witnessing Arjuna's great vision.

    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.20 Hi, indeed; idam, this; antaram, intermediate space; dyavaprthivyoh, between heaven and earth; ca, as also; sarvah, all; the disah, direction; vyaptam, are pervaded; tvaya, by You; ekena, alone, who have assumed the Cosmic form. Mahatman, O exalted One, who by nature are high-minded; the lokatrayam, three worlds; pravyathitam, are struck with fear, or are perturbed; drstva, by seeing; idam, this; abdhutam, strange, astonishing; ugram, fearful, terrible; rupam, form; tava, of Yours. Therefore, now, in order to clear that doubt which Arjuna earlier had-as in, 'whether we shall win, or whether they shall coner' (2.6)-, the Lord proceeds with the idea, 'I shall show the inevitable victory of the Pandavas.' Visualizing that, Arjuna said: 'Moreover-'.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.20 The terms, 'heaven and earth,' imply all the upper and lower worlds. The 'Antara', or that between heaven and earth, denotes the space between them in which are located all the worlds. You alone pervade all the space and all the arters. 'Beholding Your marvellous and teriible form,' beholding Your form of infinite length and extent, marvellous and terrible, the three worlds are trembling. Gods headed by Brahma, the Asuras, the manes, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, the Yaksas, and Raksasas have come with a desire to see the battle. All the 'three worlds' consisting of these friendly, antagonistic and neutral beings are extremely frightened. 'Mahatman' means one, the dimension of whose mind has no limits. It has to be understood that like Arjuna, other beings also were granted by the Lord the divine eye capable of directly perceiving the Form which supports the universe. If it be asked why, the reply is that it was for demonstrating to Arjuna His sovereignty. Hence it is stated here: 'Beholding Your marvellous and terrible form, O Mahatman, the three worlds are greatly overwhelmed with fear.'

    Personal Guidance
    You alone fill space between heaven and earth — seeing Your wondrous, terrible form, the three worlds tremble.
    Practical Applications
    • Acknowledge Kṛṣṇa's full presence — including the terrible aspect.
    • Don't sanitize the terror of cosmic vision.
    • Honor the appropriate fear (yathā-bhāva) before majesty.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I sanitized away appropriate awe?
    • What does restoring it teach?
    Analogy

    Ink dropped into water spreads until no clear water is left — yet the ink is one drop. So the Lord, one, fills the space between sky and earth, and the worlds shake not because He has multiplied but because He is everywhere at once.

    Stories
    Vāmana's Two Strides

    When Vāmanadeva took up the three steps promised by Bali (SB 8.20–21), He covered the whole earth with one stride and the whole heaven with the second — His foot reached the upper shell of the universe and pierced it. The three worlds trembled; Bali's chiefs fled in terror.

    Arjuna's verse — dyāv ā-pṛthivyor idam antaraṁ hi vyāptaṁ tvayaikena — describes the same fact in a different register. The Lord, one (ekena), fills the entire space between heaven and earth. Vāmana's stride is the visible enactment of what Arjuna now sees standing still.

    Important Words
    • sura - saṅghāḥ — hosts of demigods
      Compound: sura (demigod) + saṅgha (host). The devas are in groups, not isolated. Even the gods have communities — and the communities surrender together.
    • viśanti — they enter
      Third-person plural present. The verb is the chapter's terrible echo — viśanti will reappear in 11.27–29 for the warriors entering the mouths. Here, surrender is entering; there, destruction is entering.
    • prāñjalayaḥ — with folded hands
      Nominative plural of prāñjali (pra + añjali). The same gesture Arjuna made in 11.14 — Arjuna sees that his bodily response is being mirrored by the devas inside the form.
    • mahā - ṛṣi — great sages
      Compound: mahā + ṛṣi. The Saptarṣis and other great seers — the highest tier of human spiritual attainment — are also chanting praises, not analysing.
    • stutibhiḥ — with prayers
      Instrumental plural of stuti — 'praise-hymn.' The technical Vedic word for formal Sanskrit stotras. The mahā-ṛṣis are not improvising; they are reciting in the established register.
    • puṣkalābhiḥ — abundant, full
      Instrumental plural of puṣkala — 'full, complete.' The praise is fully-stocked, not a token gesture. Paired with stutibhiḥ, the phrase names the formal stotra-tradition given in its plenitude.
    All the hosts of demigods are surrendering before You and entering into You. Some of them, very much afraid, are offering prayers with folded hands. Hosts of great sages and perfected beings, crying “All peace!” are praying to You by singing the Vedic hymns.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण
    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.
    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Arjuna reports a cosmic spectacle: even the devas are being swallowed into the form; the frightened among them pray, while sages and siddhas extol with copious stotras. Heaven itself is both terrified and reverent — a striking reversal of ordinary devotion.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Three responses are catalogued: viśanti (helpless absorption), gṛṇanti (frightened murmured praise), stuvanti (formal stotra-recitation). 'Svasti' is the canonical Vedic peace-blessing. The verse positions the unseen heavens reacting in parallel to Arjuna's own reactions — he is the human echo of a cosmic event.

    Purport

    The demigods in all the planetary systems feared the terrific manifestation of the universal form and its glaring effulgence and so prayed for protection.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    21. This host of devatās enters into You. Some in fear praise You with folded hands. Shouting “Svasti!” the host of great sages and Siddhas praise You with excellent verses.
    Commentary

    Tvā stands for tvām.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    21. This host of devatās take shelter of You. Some in fear praise You with folded hands. Shouting “svasti!” the host of great sages and siddhas praise You with excellent verses.
    Commentary

    This host of devatās resort to You, take shelter of You (tvā viśanti). Among the devatās, some, being afraid, are standing at a distance with folded hands, praying “Please protect us, master!” The host of great sages and siddhas, seeing the great danger, (in order to pacify You), praise You, saying, “Let there be auspiciousness for the universe!”

    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    Now Arjuna describes Kala-rupa

    COMMON THEME: Text 11.19 marks the beginning of description of ‘Kala-rupa’ (The form as Time) which

    continues up till Text 11.31

    PLEASE NOTE: All points of the purports are included as the sub-points; as such there are no individual ‘Focus of

    Learning’ sections for these verses.

    

    

    ARJUNA’S FURTHER DESCRIPTION OF THE UNIVERSAL FORM AS ‘KALA-RUPA’.

    Blazing fire coming forth from your mouth, burning this entire universe (11.19)
    Numberless arms and sun and moon are the eyes
    Without origin, middle and end
    Repetition of glories is not a flaw – It is a sign of bewilderment, wonder or great ecstasy
    Spread throughout – Spread throughout the sky and planets and all space in between; and all the planetary systems are perturbed seeing you (11.20)
    ‘Dyav-a-prthivyoh’ (Space between heaven and earth) and ‘Loka-trayam’ (Three worlds) –indicate that not only Arjuna saw, but other planetary systems, whoever endowed with divine vision, also saw this form and got perturbed
    This proves that Arjuna’s seeing was not a dream
    Petitioned by demigods – Kala-rupa is petitioned by demigods and sages – All are fearful (11.21 – 11.22)
    Demigods are surrendering and praying with folded hands
    Great sages are praying with Vedic hymns
    Siva, Adityas, Vasus etc beholding You in wonder
    Rasa changes to fear – Arjuna experiences a terrible fearsome sight (11.23)
    Arjuna loses steadiness and equilibrium of mind, because mind is perturbed by fear (11.24)
    Arjuna sees blazing death-like faces and awful teeth (11.25)
    Link between texts 11.25 & 11.26: Text 11.26 through 11.30 describe future occurrences that Arjuna sees within the kala-rupa. In Text 11.7, Krishna said that Arjuna could see “whatever *he+ may want to see in the future.” In these texts, Arjuna sees that Bhisma, Drona and Karna – the three most feared members of the opposing army – will be destroyed.
    Two Analogies: Devouring all soldiers of both armies on both sides, including Bhisma, Drona & Karna, rushing into Your mouth (11.26 – 11.27)
    Analogy: As many waves of river flow into the ocean (11.28)
    Analogy: As moths dash to destruction in blazing fire (11.29*)
    Indicates that Arjuna could see his awaited victory
    All-devouring – You are devouring all people from all sides, your effulgence is covering all the universe with terrible scorching rays(11.30)

    ARJUNA’S QUESTIONS

    Arjuna in great fear asks two questions (11.31)
    Who are You?
    What is Your mission?
    Why Arjuna asks these questions – Because although Arjuna knew Krishna as his friend and Supreme Personality of Godhead, but he was puzzled by various forms exhibited by Krishna

    Personal Guidance
    All the demigods are surrendering to You; some, fearful, fold hands and offer prayers — the great sages chant Your glory.
    Practical Applications
    • Recognize that even demigods surrender to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Trust the testimony of the highest beings.
    • Don't think your skepticism is more sophisticated than their surrender.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where is my sophistication actually delusion?
    • What does demigod-level surrender teach?
    Analogy

    When the king himself enters the throne room, even his ministers and generals fold their hands. Some are afraid, some recite the formal greeting, but no one stands as a peer. The devas, full of their own power, become petitioners when the Lord's full form is exposed.

    Stories
    The Demigods at the Churning of the Ocean

    When the halāhala poison rose from the ocean during the churning (SB 8.6–7), the demigods, terrified, fled to Lord Śiva — and to Lord Viṣṇu through Brahmā — folding their hands and chanting prayers (stutibhiḥ puṣkalābhiḥ). The Bhāgavatam records the great sages and siddhas joining the chorus.

    This is the exact tableau Arjuna sees in 11.21: sura-saṅghāḥ entering, kecit bhītāḥ prāñjalayaḥ, mahā-ṛṣi-siddha-saṅghāḥ chanting svasti. The viśva-rūpa scene contains, in one frame, every such moment in cosmic history.
