    Important Words
    • rudra — the Rudras
      Eleven forms of Śiva. Their inclusion at the head of the list signals that the form Arjuna sees outranks even the destroyer-aspect of the cosmos.
    • sādhyāḥ — the Sādhyas
      A class of celestial beings associated with sacrificial perfection. Their presence indicates that even the deities of yajña are subordinate to the form.
    • gandharva — the Gandharvas
      Celestial musicians. Even music — the divine register most likely to imagine itself adequate to praise — has paused to behold.
    • asura — the demons
      Notably included. The Lord's display does not respect the asura/sura partition — both behold. Surrender will divide them later (11.36); here, wonder unites them.
    • vīkṣante — they behold
      Third-person plural present of vi-īkṣ, 'to look intently.' Not casual seeing — intent, fixed gaze. Every being on the list is locked onto the form.
    • vismitāḥ — astonished
      Past participle of vi-smi — overcome with wonder. The same emotional register Arjuna entered in 11.14; now he sees that emotion shared across the cosmos.
    All the various manifestations of Lord Śiva, the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvīs, the Maruts, the forefathers, the Gandharvas, the Yakṣas, the Asuras and the perfected demigods are beholding You in wonder.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    A second roll-call of celestial classes, now in nominative — they too watch. Even the gods are in the audience; the cosmic form is what the cosmos itself attends. Astonishment, not just terror, is the universal mood.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The list expands 11.6's catalog and adds even Asuras and Gandharvas — every metaphysical class is included. 'Uṣma-pāḥ' are pitṛs who 'drink the steam' of food-offerings (Manusmṛti 3.197). The viewing community is exhaustive, so Arjuna's unique gift (11.47) is sharpened against this universal witness-list.

    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    22. The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, Sadhyas, Viśvas, Aśvins, Maruts, Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas all look at You in astonishment.
    Commentary

    Uṣma-pā refers to those who drink hot vapor of food. That refers to the Pitṛs. The śruti says ūṣmabhāgā hi pitaraḥ: the Pitṛs eat the steam. (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, Yajur Veda, 1.3.10.6)

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    22. The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, Sadhyas, Viśvas, the Aśvins, Maruts, Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas all look at You in astonishment.
    Commentary

    This verse is clear in meaning. Uṣmapāḥ refers to the pitṛs who drink steam (uṣma). Śruti says uṣmabhāgā hi pitaraḥ: the pitṛs take the steam. (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, Yajur Veda, 1.3.10.6)

    Theme

    Now Arjuna describes Kala-rupa

    COMMON THEME: Text 11.19 marks the beginning of description of ‘Kala-rupa’ (The form as Time) which

    continues up till Text 11.31

    PLEASE NOTE: All points of the purports are included as the sub-points; as such there are no individual ‘Focus of

    Learning’ sections for these verses.

    

    

    ARJUNA’S FURTHER DESCRIPTION OF THE UNIVERSAL FORM AS ‘KALA-RUPA’.

    Blazing fire coming forth from your mouth, burning this entire universe (11.19)
    Numberless arms and sun and moon are the eyes
    Without origin, middle and end
    Repetition of glories is not a flaw – It is a sign of bewilderment, wonder or great ecstasy
    Spread throughout – Spread throughout the sky and planets and all space in between; and all the planetary systems are perturbed seeing you (11.20)
    ‘Dyav-a-prthivyoh’ (Space between heaven and earth) and ‘Loka-trayam’ (Three worlds) –indicate that not only Arjuna saw, but other planetary systems, whoever endowed with divine vision, also saw this form and got perturbed
    This proves that Arjuna’s seeing was not a dream
    Petitioned by demigods – Kala-rupa is petitioned by demigods and sages – All are fearful (11.21 – 11.22)
    Demigods are surrendering and praying with folded hands
    Great sages are praying with Vedic hymns
    Siva, Adityas, Vasus etc beholding You in wonder
    Rasa changes to fear – Arjuna experiences a terrible fearsome sight (11.23)
    Arjuna loses steadiness and equilibrium of mind, because mind is perturbed by fear (11.24)
    Arjuna sees blazing death-like faces and awful teeth (11.25)
    Link between texts 11.25 & 11.26: Text 11.26 through 11.30 describe future occurrences that Arjuna sees within the kala-rupa. In Text 11.7, Krishna said that Arjuna could see “whatever *he+ may want to see in the future.” In these texts, Arjuna sees that Bhisma, Drona and Karna – the three most feared members of the opposing army – will be destroyed.
    Two Analogies: Devouring all soldiers of both armies on both sides, including Bhisma, Drona & Karna, rushing into Your mouth (11.26 – 11.27)
    Analogy: As many waves of river flow into the ocean (11.28)
    Analogy: As moths dash to destruction in blazing fire (11.29*)
    Indicates that Arjuna could see his awaited victory
    All-devouring – You are devouring all people from all sides, your effulgence is covering all the universe with terrible scorching rays(11.30)

    ARJUNA’S QUESTIONS

    Arjuna in great fear asks two questions (11.31)
    Who are You?
    What is Your mission?
    Why Arjuna asks these questions – Because although Arjuna knew Krishna as his friend and Supreme Personality of Godhead, but he was puzzled by various forms exhibited by Krishna

    Commentary

    11.22 रुद्रादित्याः Rudras and Adityas? वसवः Vasus? ये these? च and? साध्याः Sadhyas? विश्वे Visvedevas? अश्िवनौ the two Asvins? मरुतः Maruts? च and? उष्मपाः Pitris? च and? गन्धर्वयक्षासुरसिद्धसङ्घाः hosts of Gandharvas? Yakshas? Asuras and Siddhas? वीक्षन्ते are looking at? त्वाम् Thee? विस्मिताः astonished? च and? एव even? सर्वे all.Commentary Sadhyas are a class of gods of whom Brahma is the chief.Visvedevas are ten gods who in Vedic times were considered as protectors of human beings. They were called guardians of the world. They were givers of plenty to the human beings. Their names are Krata? Daksha? Vasu? Satya? Kama? Kala? Dhvani? Rochaka? Adrava and Pururava.The two Asvins? born of Prabha (light)? daughter of Tushta and the Sun? are the physicians of the gods.Rudras? Adityas? Vasus and Maruts -- see tenth chapter? verses 21 and 23.Ushmapa A class of manes. They accept the food offered in the Sraaddha (anniversary) ceremony or the obseies? while it is hot. Hence they are called Ushmapas. There are seven groups of manes.Gandharvas are celestial singers such as Haha and Huhu.Yakshas such as Kubera (the god of wealth) Asuras such as Virochana perfected ones such as Kapila.

    Personal Guidance
    Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, Maruts, ancestors — all are awestruck, beholding You.
    Practical Applications
    • Recognize the universal awe; you are not alone in being humbled.
    • Use this verse during personal humbling moments.
    • Don't perform false composure when awe is appropriate.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I performed composure instead of feeling awe?
    • What honest awe is being asked?
    Analogy

    Imagine an opera in which the entire orchestra, every chorus, every soloist has gone silent and is staring at the stage. That is the moment of 11.22 — every category of celestial being, even the asuras, has stopped its function to behold one form.

    Stories
    The Reverence of Even the Asuras

    When Lord Nṛsiṁha appeared from the pillar (SB 7.8), even the demons who served Hiraṇyakaśipu fell silent, struck with wonder. Their hostility did not dissolve — Hiraṇyakaśipu still rushed at the Lord — but the spectacle itself momentarily suspended the categories.

    Arjuna's catalogue in 11.22 includes asura-siddha-saṅghāḥ alongside the devas and sages. Even the demons are vīkṣante vismitāḥ — beholding in wonder. The viśva-rūpa silences hostility long enough to be seen.

    Important Words
    • vaktra — mouth
      Compound element repeated through the verse. The mouths are now stressed because they are about to become devouring (verses 25–30). Vocabulary thickens around the form's terrible aspect.
    • mahā - bāho — O mighty-armed
      Vocative — an epithet Arjuna himself usually receives. Here Arjuna applies it to Kṛṣṇa, surrendering even his own warrior-title to the form before him.
    • bahu - daṁṣṭrā — many-toothed
      Compound: many + tooth/fang. Daṁṣṭrā is specifically the fang — predatory, not vegetarian. The lexicon is now openly that of a devouring being.
    • karālam — terrible
      Adjective from kṛ — 'doing fearful things.' Karāla becomes a standard epithet of Kālī and other fierce forms; Arjuna invokes it here for the cosmic form.
    • pravyathitāḥ — perturbed
      Same root as 11.20 — the trembling intensifies. The worlds were perturbed; now Arjuna joins them. The grammar is precise: tathā aham — 'so am I.'
    O mighty-armed one, all the planets with their demigods are disturbed at seeing Your great form, with its many faces, eyes, arms, thighs, legs and bellies and Your many terrible teeth; and as they are disturbed, so am I.

    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.
    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    The fang-detail enters: 'bahu-daṁṣṭrā-karālam.' What was wondrous in 11.10-11 turns frightful. Arjuna lets slip his own state — 'tathā 'ham' — admitting that he is no longer just a witness; he is among the disturbed.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Pivot verse from awe to terror. The compound 'daṁṣṭrā-karāla' becomes the keyword of the next several verses (11.25, 11.27). 'Tathā 'ham' is the personal disclosure: in 11.20 only loka-traya was pravyathita; now Arjuna is too. The vocative 'mahā-bāho' (mighty-armed) — usually flattery — now sounds ominous when the arms in question are countless and gripping weapons.

    23. O mighty-armed one, seeing this great form with many mouths and eyes, many arms, many thighs and feet, many stomachs, fearful with many teeth, the world and I as well are filled with terror.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    23. O mighty-armed one, seeing this great form with many mouths and eyes, many arms, thighs and feet, many stomachs, fearful with many teeth, the world is filled with terror.
    Commentary

    This verse concludes the description of the three worlds being agitated on seeing the form. This form was ferocious (karālam) with many teeth. The rest of the verse is clear. The last phrase tathāham (I also) is connected to the next verse as the subject.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Now Arjuna starts to see the fear even of the demigods, he also becomes affraid. His rasa changes from wonder (adbhuta) to fear (bhaya).

    Theme

    Now Arjuna describes Kala-rupa

    COMMON THEME: Text 11.19 marks the beginning of description of ‘Kala-rupa’ (The form as Time) which

    continues up till Text 11.31

    PLEASE NOTE: All points of the purports are included as the sub-points; as such there are no individual ‘Focus of

    

    

    ARJUNA’S FURTHER DESCRIPTION OF THE UNIVERSAL FORM AS ‘KALA-RUPA’.

    Blazing fire coming forth from your mouth, burning this entire universe (11.19)
    Numberless arms and sun and moon are the eyes
    Without origin, middle and end
    Repetition of glories is not a flaw – It is a sign of bewilderment, wonder or great ecstasy
    Spread throughout – Spread throughout the sky and planets and all space in between; and all the planetary systems are perturbed seeing you (11.20)
    ‘Dyav-a-prthivyoh’ (Space between heaven and earth) and ‘Loka-trayam’ (Three worlds) –indicate that not only Arjuna saw, but other planetary systems, whoever endowed with divine vision, also saw this form and got perturbed
    This proves that Arjuna’s seeing was not a dream
    Petitioned by demigods – Kala-rupa is petitioned by demigods and sages – All are fearful (11.21 – 11.22)
    Demigods are surrendering and praying with folded hands
    Great sages are praying with Vedic hymns
    Siva, Adityas, Vasus etc beholding You in wonder
    Rasa changes to fear – Arjuna experiences a terrible fearsome sight (11.23)
    Arjuna loses steadiness and equilibrium of mind, because mind is perturbed by fear (11.24)
    Arjuna sees blazing death-like faces and awful teeth (11.25)
    Link between texts 11.25 & 11.26: Text 11.26 through 11.30 describe future occurrences that Arjuna sees within the kala-rupa. In Text 11.7, Krishna said that Arjuna could see “whatever *he+ may want to see in the future.” In these texts, Arjuna sees that Bhisma, Drona and Karna – the three most feared members of the opposing army – will be destroyed.
    Two Analogies: Devouring all soldiers of both armies on both sides, including Bhisma, Drona & Karna, rushing into Your mouth (11.26 – 11.27)
    Analogy: As many waves of river flow into the ocean (11.28)
    Analogy: As moths dash to destruction in blazing fire (11.29*)
    Indicates that Arjuna could see his awaited victory
    All-devouring – You are devouring all people from all sides, your effulgence is covering all the universe with terrible scorching rays(11.30)

    ARJUNA’S QUESTIONS

    Arjuna in great fear asks two questions (11.31)
    Who are You?
    What is Your mission?
    Why Arjuna asks these questions – Because although Arjuna knew Krishna as his friend and Supreme Personality of Godhead, but he was puzzled by various forms exhibited by Krishna

    Personal Guidance
    Seeing Your great form with many mouths and eyes, many arms and thighs — all the worlds are perturbed, as I am.
    Practical Applications
    • Recognize that even Arjuna is perturbed by this vision.
    • Don't expect spiritual vision to always be soothing.
    • Honor the disturbance as a stage.
    Reflection Questions
    • When has spiritual encounter disturbed me?
    • Did I treat it as failure or stage?
    Analogy

    A peasant who has never left his valley meets the army of his emperor — every regiment, every general, every weapon — and he trembles as the worlds tremble. Arjuna sees the cosmos trembling, and his own self, made of the cosmos, trembles in unison.

    Important Words
    • nabhaḥ - spṛśam — touching the sky
      Compound: nabhas (sky) + spṛś (touch). Used in the Mahābhārata for Hanumān's mountain-leap; here for the cosmic body's reach. The form's height is at the limit of the firmament itself.
    • vyātta — wide-opened
      Past participle of vi-ā-tan, 'stretched apart.' The mouths are wide-opened — the prelude to the devouring in verses 27–30. The participle marks the apertures' state.
    • pravyathita — perturbed
      Past participle of pra-vyath — 'thoroughly distressed.' Modifies antaḥ-ātmā. The disturbance reaches the deepest stratum Arjuna can name.
    • dhṛtim — steadiness
      From dhṛ — 'to hold.' Dhṛti is the steady-holding faculty by which the mind keeps its shape. It is one of the qualities Kṛṣṇa will later praise in chapter 18; here Arjuna confesses its temporary loss.
    • śamam — peace
      From śam — 'to be calm.' Śama is one of the six treasures (ṣaṭ-sampatti) of the sādhaka; Arjuna admits he has lost it. Honest report, not theological failure.
    • viṣṇo — O Viṣṇu
      Vocative. Arjuna shifts his address from Kṛṣṇa to Viṣṇu at the moment of greatest fear — the cosmic-pervading aspect is foregrounded over the personal-friend aspect.
    O all-pervading Viṣṇu, seeing You with Your many radiant colors touching the sky, Your gaping mouths, and Your great glowing eyes, my mind is perturbed by fear. I can no longer maintain my steadiness or equilibrium of mind.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण
    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.
    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Arjuna confesses what the previous verses circled: he has lost both dhṛti (composure) and śama (inner peace). The vocative 'Viṣṇu' — the all-pervader — reminds Kṛṣṇa that the all-pervadingness Arjuna asked to see is now unbearable.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    First explicit collapse of Arjuna's equilibrium under the vision. Compare 1.29-30, where his earlier collapse was caused by kinship-attachment; this one is caused by an excess of theological vision. The Gītā thus stages two breakdowns — the second now reframed by all that has been taught between. The lost dhṛti will be addressed by Kṛṣṇa's command 'mā vyathiṣṭhāḥ' in 11.34.

    Translation
    24. O Viṣṇu, seeing You touch the heavens, shining in many colors, with gaping mouth, and wide, blazing eyes, I have become distressed in mind, and do not find any satisfaction or relief.
    Commentary

    Śama means relief or tranquility.

    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    24. O Viṣṇu, seeing You touch the heavens, shining in many colors, with gaping mouth, and wide, blazing eyes, I as well have become fearful in mind, and do not find any satisfaction or relief.
    Commentary

    Arjuna expresses his pitiful state in two verses so that the Lord will withdraw this form. Seeing You, I have become mentally agitated with fear, and do not attain satisfaction (dhṛtim) or peace (śamam), O Viṣṇu! What is this form? It touches the sky, spreads into the antarikṣa (nabhaḥ spṛśam), and has gaping mouth (vyāttānanam). The meaning of the rest of the words is clear. Here Arjuna expresses his rasa of fear, caused by seeing the Lord’s form as time.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The form was touching the sky. As far as Arjuna looked he could only see the sky. In that sense that form was touching the sky.

    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.24 O Visnu, hi, verily; drstva, seeing; tvam, You; nabhah-sprsam, touching heaven; diptam, blazing; aneka-varnam, with many colours, (i.e.) possessed of many frightening forms; vyatta-ananam, open-mouthed; dipta-visala-netram, with firey large eyes; I, pravyathita-antara-atma, becoming terrified in my mind; na vindami, do not find; dhrtim, steadiness; ca, and; samam, peace, calmness of mind. Why?
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.24 The term 'Nabhas' denotes the Supreme Heaven (Parama-Vyoman), which is beyond the Prakrti composed of the three Gunas as established by the Sruti passages such as: 'That is in the Imperishable Supreme Heaven' (Ma. Na. U., 1.2), 'Him, sun-coloured and beyond Tamas' (Sve., 3.8) 'The dweller beyond the Rajas' (Rg. S., 2.6.25.5) and 'He who is the president in the Supreme Heaven' (Rg. S., 8.9.17.7). This can be understood as implied in the statement that 'the form touches the Supreme Heaven.' It expresses the idea that it is the foundation of all - of the principle of the Prakrti with its conditions, and of the individual selves in all states. It has also been initially declared: 'For by You alone are pervaded the interspace of heaven and earth ৷৷.' (11.20). 'Beholding Your form shining, multicoloured, and with yawning mouths and large and resplendent eyes, my inner being trembles in fear. I am unable to find support, namely, I am unable to find support for the body. I am unable to get peace of mind and of the senses. O Visnu, namely, O Pervader, beholding You pervading everything, incomparable in magnitude, extremely wonderful and terrible, I find my limbs ivering and my senses agitated.' Such is the meaning.
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical
    Translation
    11.24 Sri Abhinavagupta did not comment upon this sloka.
    Swami Sivananda Classical
    Translation
    11.24 On seeing Thee (the Cosmic Form) touching the sky, shining in many colours, with mouths wide open, with large fiery eyes, I am terrified at heart and find neither courage nor peace, O Vishnu.

    11.24 नभःस्पृशम् touching the sky? दीप्तम् shining? अनेकवर्णम् in many colours? व्यात्ताननम् with mouths wide open? दीप्तविशालनेत्रम् with larve fiery eyes? दृष्ट्वा having seen? हि verily? त्वाम् Thee? प्रव्यथितान्तरात्मा terrified at heart? धृतिम् courage? न not? विन्दामि (I) find? शमम् peace? च and? विष्णो O Vishnu.Commentary Dhriti also means patience and strength. Sama also means control.The vision of the Cosmic Form has frightened Arjuna considerably.

    Personal Guidance
    Seeing You touching the sky, blazing with many colors, with widely opened mouths — my heart is shaken; I cannot find composure.
    Practical Applications
    • Honor the moments when spiritual encounter shakes you.
    • Don't rush to composure; receive the shaking.
    • Trust that composure returns after the encounter integrates.
    Reflection Questions
    • When was I last shaken by spiritual reality?
    • What did the integration teach?
    Analogy

    A small boat in a great storm is not capsized by malice but simply by scale. Arjuna's mind is the small boat; the form is the storm; his loss of dhṛti is not failure of discipline but proper recognition of disproportion.

    Important Words
    • daṁṣṭrā — teeth
      Nominative. The fangs again, now in close-up — Arjuna is looking directly at them rather than describing the body from a distance.
    • karālāni — terrible
      Same root as 11.23; here in the neuter plural agreeing with mukhāni. The terribleness has shifted from form to face.
    • kāla - anala — fire of cosmic time
      Compound: kāla (time) + anala (fire). The Mahābhārata's technical name for the dissolution-fire. Arjuna labels what he sees by its proper apocalyptic title.
    • sannibhāni — resembling
      Neuter plural of sannibha — 'with the appearance of.' Like 11.12's sadṛśī, the verse marks resemblance rather than identity. Even at peak terror, Arjuna's diction stays precise.
    • prasīda — be gracious
      Imperative of pra-sad. The single-word petition that will be repeated in 11.31, 11.45, and 11.46. The chapter's most-used verb of supplication.
    • jagat - nivāsa — refuge of the worlds
      Vocative compound: jagat (world) + nivāsa (dwelling, resting-place). Arjuna names the Lord by His function of giving shelter at the moment he most desperately needs it.
    O Lord of lords, O refuge of the worlds, please be gracious to me. I cannot keep my balance seeing thus Your blazing deathlike faces and awful teeth. In all directions I am bewildered.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण
    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.
    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    First explicit 'prasīda' of the chapter. The simile 'kāla-anala-sannibha' (resembling the fire of Time) plants the keyword kāla which Kṛṣṇa will pick up in 11.32. Arjuna has lost orientation itself — directions vanish.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    'Kāla-anala' is the saṁvartaka-agni, the fire of cosmic dissolution. By comparing Kṛṣṇa's mouths to it, Arjuna unwittingly anticipates Kṛṣṇa's self-identification as Time-the-destroyer (11.32). 'Diśo na jāne' is bodily disorientation — pre-rational panic; he prays for grace before continuing description. 'Jagan-nivāsa' reminds: my refuge is also You.

    he deva-īśa! he jagat-nivāsa! daṃṣṭrā-karālāni kāla-anala-sannibhāni te mukhāni dṛṣṭvā eva diśaḥ na jāne, śarma ca na labhe; prasīda |
    O Lord of gods, O abode of the universe! Just at seeing Your fang-dreadful mouths, like the fires of cosmic dissolution, I know not the directions and I find no comfort. Be gracious!

    Translation
    25. Seeing Your mouth with sharp teeth, like the fire of cosmic destruction, I cannot recognize the directions and I feel no comfort. O master of the devas, abode of the universe, be merciful to me. 26-27. All the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with the host of rulers of the earth, Bhīṣma, Droṇa and Karṇa, together with our prominent warriors, enter swiftly into Your fearful mouth with sharp teeth. Some, with their heads ground up, are sticking between Your teeth.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    25. Seeing Your mouths with sharp teeth, like the fire of cosmic destruction, I cannot recognize the directions and I feel no comfort. O master of the devas, abode of the universe, be merciful to me. 26-27. All the sons of Dhṛtarāsṭṛa along with the host of rulers of the earth, Bhiṣma, Droṇa and Karṇa, together with our prominent warriors, enter swiftly into Your fearful mouth with sharp teeth. Some, with their heads ground up, are sticking between Your teeth.
    Commentary

    Seeing Your ferocious teeth and mouths, which are similar (saṁnibhāni) to the fire of destruction at the end of the universe (kalānala), [Note: This was described as one of Kṛṣṇa’s vibhūtis in the last chapter, verse 33.] (I do not recognize the directions), and I find no comfort (śarma).     The Lord previously said “See whatever else you desire to see.” The Lord meant, “See in My body the future victory and defeat in this war.” Now he shows this in five verses. All these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana and others, along with the gathering of kings (avani pāla) such as Śalya and Jayadratha, and that son of a charioteer, Karṇa (asau sūta putraḥ) are swiftly entering Your mouths. And even those who are famous as undefeatable, like Bhīṣma, are entering Your mouths. Asau used with sūta putraḥ indicates “Karṇa has held continuous hatred of me (Arjuna).” Not only those, but they enter Your mouths even with our chief warriors such as Dhṛṣṭadhyumna. The ornament sahokti is used. [Note: In the case of being sahokti, the sentence would suggest that the chief warriors are causing the enemy to enter the mouths.] Among them, some are seen to be stuck between the teeth of that universal form, with their heads (uttamaḥ aṅgaiḥ) crushed. This is what I see.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Arjuna's rasa is turning to bewiderement. Earlier in this chapter Krsna said: "See all this in just one part of My body." But as soon as Arjuna was actually seeing the universal form, he forgot he couldn't see Krsna's body anymore, he could only see the universal form.

    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    Now Arjuna describes Kala-rupa

    COMMON THEME: Text 11.19 marks the beginning of description of ‘Kala-rupa’ (The form as Time) which

    continues up till Text 11.31

    PLEASE NOTE: All points of the purports are included as the sub-points; as such there are no individual ‘Focus of

    Learning’ sections for these verses.

    

    

    ARJUNA’S FURTHER DESCRIPTION OF THE UNIVERSAL FORM AS ‘KALA-RUPA’.

    Blazing fire coming forth from your mouth, burning this entire universe (11.19)
    Numberless arms and sun and moon are the eyes
    Without origin, middle and end
    Repetition of glories is not a flaw – It is a sign of bewilderment, wonder or great ecstasy
    Spread throughout – Spread throughout the sky and planets and all space in between; and all the planetary systems are perturbed seeing you (11.20)
    ‘Dyav-a-prthivyoh’ (Space between heaven and earth) and ‘Loka-trayam’ (Three worlds) –indicate that not only Arjuna saw, but other planetary systems, whoever endowed with divine vision, also saw this form and got perturbed
    This proves that Arjuna’s seeing was not a dream
    Petitioned by demigods – Kala-rupa is petitioned by demigods and sages – All are fearful (11.21 – 11.22)
    Demigods are surrendering and praying with folded hands
    Great sages are praying with Vedic hymns
    Siva, Adityas, Vasus etc beholding You in wonder
    Rasa changes to fear – Arjuna experiences a terrible fearsome sight (11.23)
    Arjuna loses steadiness and equilibrium of mind, because mind is perturbed by fear (11.24)
    Arjuna sees blazing death-like faces and awful teeth (11.25)
    Link between texts 11.25 & 11.26: Text 11.26 through 11.30 describe future occurrences that Arjuna sees within the kala-rupa. In Text 11.7, Krishna said that Arjuna could see “whatever *he+ may want to see in the future.” In these texts, Arjuna sees that Bhisma, Drona and Karna – the three most feared members of the opposing army – will be destroyed.
    Two Analogies: Devouring all soldiers of both armies on both sides, including Bhisma, Drona & Karna, rushing into Your mouth (11.26 – 11.27)
    Analogy: As many waves of river flow into the ocean (11.28)
    Analogy: As moths dash to destruction in blazing fire (11.29*)
    Indicates that Arjuna could see his awaited victory
    All-devouring – You are devouring all people from all sides, your effulgence is covering all the universe with terrible scorching rays(11.30)

    ARJUNA’S QUESTIONS

    Arjuna in great fear asks two questions (11.31)
    Who are You?
    What is Your mission?
    Why Arjuna asks these questions – Because although Arjuna knew Krishna as his friend and Supreme Personality of Godhead, but he was puzzled by various forms exhibited by Krishna

    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.25 Drstva eva, having merely seen; te, Your; mukhani, mouths; damstra-karalani, made terrible with (their) teeth; and kala-anala-sannibhani, resembling the fire of Dissolution is kalanala; similar to that; na jane, I have lost; the sense of disah, direction-I do not know the directions as to which is East or which is West; and hence, na labhe, find no; sarma, comfort. Therefore, prasida, be gracious; devesa, O Lord of gods; jagannivasa, O Abode of the Universe! 'The apprehension which was there of my getting defeated by those offers, that too has cleared away, since-'
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.25 Looking at Your mouths, extremely terrifying and like cosmic fire at the end of the universe, and operating for the destruction of everything, I have lost the sense of recognising the arters of the sky, nor do I feel happy and peaceful. O Abode of all the worlds, O Lord of all the Devas, namely, O Overlord of even gods like Brahma! Be gracious unto me. The meaning is: 'Do act in such a way that I may attain my natural condition. Arjuna's charioteer (Parthasarathi), thus showing that all the worlds depend upon Him for their existence and activities, showed to the son of Prtha (Arjuna) that what He wanted to do, making Arjuna a mere instrument of His, was to lighten the burden of the earth through the destruction of all those who were of Asuric manifestations and who, in the guise of kings, were presenting themselves as the sons of Dhrtarastra and their followers. Many such embodiments of Asuras were present also in the ranks of Yudhisthira's followers. And Arjuna, after having realised with the divine eyes, received through His grace, the complete manifestation of the Lord as the Creator etc., witnessed also the slaughter of the followers of the sons of Dhrtarastra etc., in that Lord Himself, who is the Self of all, even though it (the slaughter) had not happened actually according to human calculations. Arjuna continues:

    11.25 Sri Abhinavagupta did not comment upon this sloka.
    Swami Sivananda Classical

    11.25 Having seen Thy mouths fearful with teeth (blazing) like the fires of cosmic dissolution, I know not the four arters, nor do I find peace. Have mercy, O Lord of the gods, O abode of the universe.
    Commentary

    11.25 दंष्ट्राकरालानि fearful with teeth? च and? ते Thy? मुखानि mouths? दृष्ट्वा having seen? एव even? कालानलसन्निभानि blazing like Pralayafires? दिशः the four arters? न not? जाने know? न not? लभे do (I) obtain? च and? शर्म peace? प्रसीद have mercy? देवेश O Lord of the gods? जगन्निवास O abode of the universe.Commentary Jagannivasa The substratum of the universe.Kalanala The fires which consume the worlds during the final dissolution of the worlds (Pralaya). Time (Kala) is the consumer of all that is manifest.Diso no jane I do not know the four arters. I cannot distinguish the east from the west? nor the north from the south.

    Swami Gambhīrānanda Classical

    Personal Guidance
    Seeing Your terrible mouths with frightful teeth — like the fire of cosmic dissolution — I lose my bearings; have mercy, Lord of lords.
    Practical Applications
    • Cry out for mercy when cosmic vision overwhelms.
    • Don't pretend you can absorb everything Kṛṣṇa shows.
    • Acknowledge limit and ask for protection.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do I pretend I can handle what overwhelms me?
    • What does asking for mercy open?
    Analogy

    When you look up at a wildfire racing across a hillside, you do not first calculate hectares — you turn your face. Arjuna, looking at faces that resemble the fire of cosmic dissolution, does the same; he hides his bearings and begs for mercy.

    Stories
    Mārkaṇḍeya at Pralaya

    The sage Mārkaṇḍeya, granted long life, witnessed the cosmic dissolution — kāla-anala, the fire of time — sweep across all the worlds (Mahābhārata, Vana-parva 188; SB 12.9). He drifted alone on the waters of pralaya, calling out to the Lord, until Lord Nārāyaṇa appeared as a child on a banyan leaf and took him into His body.

    Arjuna's word in 11.25 — kāla-anala-sannibhāni, like the fire of cosmic time — is precisely Mārkaṇḍeya's vision. Arjuna does not invent the simile; he is recognising a category the tradition already knows.

    Important Words
    • bhīṣmaḥ — Bhīṣma
      Nominative — named. The grandsire is not a general category but a specific person Arjuna loves, and Arjuna sees him by name entering the mouths. The vision is unsparing in its particularity.
    • droṇaḥ — Droṇa
      Nominative — named. Arjuna's own teacher of archery. The verse will not let Arjuna shelter behind abstractions; the persons most dear to him are named first.
    • sūta - putraḥ — the son of a charioteer (Karṇa)
      Compound: charioteer + son. The Mahābhārata's standard epithet for Karṇa, recalling his caste-charged identity. Even Karṇa, Arjuna's secret elder brother, is named within.
    • tvaramāṇāḥ — rushing
      Present participle of tvar, 'to hurry.' The warriors are not pulled — they hurry. Even at the moment of being devoured, the agency of the doomed is preserved, which is theologically important.
    • viśanti — they enter
      Same verb as 11.21, now applied to warriors instead of devas. Both surrender and destruction are 'entering' the Lord — only the angle differs.
    • cūrṇitaiḥ — with smashed (heads)
      Instrumental plural of cūrṇita, past participle of cūrṇ, 'to grind to powder.' The vocabulary is unsoftened; the Gītā does not aestheticise war.
    All the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with their allied kings, and Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa – and our chief soldiers also – are rushing into Your fearful mouths. And some I see trapped with heads smashed between Your teeth.

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Now Arjuna sees his own war: Duryodhana's sons, allied kings, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, even his own side's chiefs — all are rushing into Kṛṣṇa's mouths. The cosmic dissolution becomes specific. The war's outcome is shown already enacted in the vision.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Dual-verse Upajāti tableau — the war that has not yet happened on Kurukṣetra is shown completed inside the form. The particularity (named warriors, including beloved Bhīṣma and Droṇa) shocks Arjuna into recognizing that the form's destruction is not abstract eschatology but his immediate situation. This is the dramatic ground for Kṛṣṇa's 'mayaivaite nihatāḥ pūrvam eva' (11.33).

    Purport

    In a previous verse the Lord promised to show Arjuna things he would be very interested in seeing. Now Arjuna sees that the leaders of the opposite party (Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa and all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra) and their soldiers and Arjuna’s own soldiers are all being annihilated. This is an indication that after the death of nearly all the persons assembled at Kurukṣetra, Arjuna will emerge victorious. It is also mentioned here that Bhīṣma, who is supposed to be unconquerable, will also be smashed. So also Karṇa. Not only will the great warriors of the other party like Bhīṣma be smashed, but some of the great warriors of Arjuna’s side also.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Krsna had said to Arjuna that he would be able to see the future too. All the great fighters and soldiers in the opposing side, that Arjuna feared, are going to be killed.

    Theme

    Now Arjuna describes Kala-rupa

    COMMON THEME: Text 11.19 marks the beginning of description of ‘Kala-rupa’ (The form as Time) which

    continues up till Text 11.31

    PLEASE NOTE: All points of the purports are included as the sub-points; as such there are no individual ‘Focus of

    Learning’ sections for these verses.

    

    

    ARJUNA’S FURTHER DESCRIPTION OF THE UNIVERSAL FORM AS ‘KALA-RUPA’.

    Blazing fire coming forth from your mouth, burning this entire universe (11.19)
    Numberless arms and sun and moon are the eyes
    Without origin, middle and end
    Repetition of glories is not a flaw – It is a sign of bewilderment, wonder or great ecstasy
    Spread throughout – Spread throughout the sky and planets and all space in between; and all the planetary systems are perturbed seeing you (11.20)
    ‘Dyav-a-prthivyoh’ (Space between heaven and earth) and ‘Loka-trayam’ (Three worlds) –indicate that not only Arjuna saw, but other planetary systems, whoever endowed with divine vision, also saw this form and got perturbed
    This proves that Arjuna’s seeing was not a dream
    Petitioned by demigods – Kala-rupa is petitioned by demigods and sages – All are fearful (11.21 – 11.22)
    Demigods are surrendering and praying with folded hands
    Great sages are praying with Vedic hymns
    Siva, Adityas, Vasus etc beholding You in wonder
    Rasa changes to fear – Arjuna experiences a terrible fearsome sight (11.23)
    Arjuna loses steadiness and equilibrium of mind, because mind is perturbed by fear (11.24)
    Arjuna sees blazing death-like faces and awful teeth (11.25)
    Link between texts 11.25 & 11.26: Text 11.26 through 11.30 describe future occurrences that Arjuna sees within the kala-rupa. In Text 11.7, Krishna said that Arjuna could see “whatever *he+ may want to see in the future.” In these texts, Arjuna sees that Bhisma, Drona and Karna – the three most feared members of the opposing army – will be destroyed.
    Two Analogies: Devouring all soldiers of both armies on both sides, including Bhisma, Drona & Karna, rushing into Your mouth (11.26 – 11.27)
    Analogy: As many waves of river flow into the ocean (11.28)
    Analogy: As moths dash to destruction in blazing fire (11.29*)
    Indicates that Arjuna could see his awaited victory
    All-devouring – You are devouring all people from all sides, your effulgence is covering all the universe with terrible scorching rays(11.30)

    ARJUNA’S QUESTIONS

    Arjuna in great fear asks two questions (11.31)
    Who are You?
    What is Your mission?
    Why Arjuna asks these questions – Because although Arjuna knew Krishna as his friend and Supreme Personality of Godhead, but he was puzzled by various forms exhibited by Krishna

    Personal Guidance
    All the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the kings of the earth, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, our chief warriors — entering Your fearful mouths, ground between Your teeth.
    Practical Applications
    • Recognize that Kṛṣṇa is already accomplishing what we fear we must accomplish.
    • Trust that the cosmic plan unfolds.
    • Stop carrying the weight you don't actually carry.
    Reflection Questions
    • What weight am I carrying that's not actually mine?
    • What does Kṛṣṇa's accomplishment release?
    Analogy

    Watching a great waterfall from the cliff, you do not see individual drops — you see the river going over. Arjuna sees Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, the chief warriors of both sides going over the edge into the mouths — a continuous river of human life pouring into the Lord's fangs.

    Stories
    The Foretold Death of Bhīṣma

    Long before Kurukṣetra, Bhīṣma had received the boon of dying only at his chosen time (icchā-mṛtyu) from his father Śantanu (Mahābhārata, Ādi-parva 100). At Kurukṣetra he chose to fall when Śikhaṇḍī faced him (Bhīṣma-parva 119). What looked like Arjuna's arrows ending Bhīṣma was already, beforehand, Bhīṣma's own choice — and behind that choice, the Lord's arrangement.

    Arjuna's vision in 11.26–27 of Bhīṣma already entering Kṛṣṇa's mouths shows him the truth: the deaths he is about to deal have already been dealt by Time.

    Important Words
    • nadīnām — of rivers
      Genitive plural. Multiple rivers, one ocean — the image's force lies in the many-to-one collapse.
    • ambu - vegāḥ — currents of water
      Compound: ambu (water) + vega (force, speed). Not still water — running water with its own velocity. The warriors have momentum; the image preserves it.
    • samudram — the ocean
      Accusative — direction of motion. Samudra is 'great-gathering,' the place where all waters are received. The Lord's mouths play the ocean's part.
    • abhimukhāḥ — facing toward
      Compound: abhi (toward) + mukha (face). The rivers face the ocean before they enter — their orientation is set before their arrival. So the warriors face death before reaching it.
    • dravanti — they flow
      Third-person plural of dru, 'to run.' Active verb — the rivers run, not drift. The motion is rapid, not contemplative.
    • abhivijvalanti — blaze brightly
      From abhi-vi-jval, 'to blaze in every direction.' The mouths blaze even as they receive. Reception and destruction are simultaneous, not sequential.
    As the many waves of the rivers flow into the ocean, so do all these great warriors enter blazing into Your mouths.

    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    First of two parallel similes for the same image. Rivers do not choose the ocean — they simply flow there; so warriors are swept toward Kṛṣṇa's mouths by an inevitability that is not their own choice. Fate is depicted as fluid dynamics.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The river-to-ocean image was the Upaniṣadic emblem of jīva-merging-into-brahman (Praśna 6.5, Chāndogya 6.10). Here it is redeployed for kāla-driven destruction: the same metaphysical movement is now dread. The simile drains the warriors of agency, preparing the doctrinal point of 11.33 that they are 'already killed.'

    Translation
    28. As many swift currents of rivers flow towards the sea, so these heroes of the world enter Your flaming mouths.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    28. As many swift currents of rivers flow towards the sea, so these heroes of the world enter Your flaming mouths.
    Commentary

    Two examples are given to describe their entering the mouths in two verses. In the first example they enter unintentionally, without understanding it. In the second example, they enter knowingly.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Two different analogies are used here: (1) as the waves of the rivers flow into the ocean and (2) 'the warriors enter into Your mouths ‑ like moths enter into the fire'. There is actually a difference between the two. 'The rivers enter into the ocean' in an inconscious way, they just flow right in. That is compared to Bhisma and Drona. They lose all their material qualities and entered Krsna's abode even though they entered in His mouth. But on the other hand 'moths' consciously enter into the fire and they are like Duryodhana who is consciously entering into his destruction.

    Personal Guidance
    As rivers flow into the ocean — so the heroes of this world enter Your blazing mouths.
    Practical Applications
    • Hold the river-into-ocean image during worry about world events.
    • Recognize the natural flow.
    • Don't dam what is already flowing.
    Reflection Questions
    • What flow am I trying to dam?
    • What does letting it flow teach?
    Analogy

    Rivers do not choose the sea; the sea simply is downhill. So the warriors do not choose the Lord's mouths — the slope of time runs that way, and they pour in by gravity, by the geometry of the cosmos, not by their own will alone.

    Stories
    Rivers Returning to the Sea — Bhāgavatam's Image

    The Bhāgavatam repeatedly uses the river-to-ocean image for the soul's return to the Lord (e.g., SB 1.10.6, 4.21.32) — as rivers naturally seek the sea, so all beings naturally tend toward the Supreme.

    Kṛṣṇa here uses the same image with reversed valence: the warriors flow into His mouths not as souls into liberation but as bodies into death. The Bhāgavatam's image is therefore comprehensive — every river reaches the sea, whether by mokṣa or by kāla. The destination is one; the mode differs.

    Important Words
    • pradīptam — blazing
      Past participle of pra-dīp, 'to flame forth.' Pra intensifies — not merely lit, but blazing high. The flame is at maximum draw.
    • jvalanam — fire
      Neuter noun from jval, 'to burn.' The general word for fire; here it is the consuming aspect of the universal form.
    • pataṅgāḥ — moths
      Nominative plural. The classical Indic example of self-destructive attraction — pataṅga appears in this sense throughout Sanskrit literature (Mahābhārata, Bhāgavatam, Bhartṛhari).
    • nāśāya — for destruction
      Dative — 'for the sake of destruction.' Repeated twice in the verse. The grammar marks purpose: the moths' goal is destruction, and so is the warriors'.
    • samṛddha — with full
      Past participle of sam-ṛdh, 'to grow completely.' Sam-ṛddha-vega is fully-grown speed — the warriors are at their peak strength precisely when they enter the mouths.
    • vegāḥ — speed
      Nominative plural. Repeated with samṛddha. The vocabulary of energy is preserved — these are not sluggish creatures, they are at full pace.
    I see all people rushing full speed into Your mouths, as moths dash to destruction in a blazing fire.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण
    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.
    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    The second simile: moths to flame. Unlike rivers (purposive flow), moths blindly mistake their own destruction for attraction. The image accuses the warriors not of choosing wrongly but of charging blindly into what will end them.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    Where 11.28's simile was neutral (rivers), this one is darker — pataṅgāḥ are emblems of self-destroying desire. Together the two similes (28 and 29) span the spectrum: ineluctable fate and blind eagerness, both arriving at the same end. The doctrinal payoff is that Arjuna's war is not the cause but the witness of a destruction already underway.

    Personal Guidance
    As moths rush into the flames of fire to be destroyed — so all the worlds rush into Your mouths to be destroyed.
    Practical Applications
    • See the moth-to-flame quality of material life.
    • Pause your own rushing toward what destroys.
    • Use this image to break automatic patterns.
    Reflection Questions
    • What flame am I rushing toward as a moth?
    • What stops me midway?
    Analogy

    A moth flying into a flame does not see the flame as enemy; it sees only the light. So men rushing into the Lord's mouths do not see Death; they see what looks like glory. The image is not a slander on the warriors — it is a diagnosis of all material striving.

    Stories
    Hiraṇyakaśipu's Rush at Nṛsiṁha

    When Hiraṇyakaśipu, in the height of his power, rushed at Lord Nṛsiṁha (SB 7.8) to destroy Him, he was not running away from death — he was running toward what he could not see was his end. The Bhāgavatam describes him as samṛddha-vega, full of momentum, rushing with sword raised.

    Kṛṣṇa's image in 11.29 of moths racing into flames — pataṅgāḥ samṛddha-vegāḥ — captures the same pattern: full force, wrong direction, eager destruction. Material energy at peak is precisely what hurls itself into the Lord's mouths.

    Important Words
    • lelihyase — You are licking
      Third-person frequentative of lih — 'to lick repeatedly.' The intensive (yaṅluganta) form marks continuous, repeated action. The Lord is not licking once; He is in the perpetual mode of licking.
    • grasamānaḥ — devouring
      Present participle of gras, 'to swallow.' Continuous aspect — devouring while licking, not afterwards. Two simultaneous actions of the cosmic mouth.
    • samantāt — from all sides
      Adverb — 'all around.' The devouring is omni-directional; there is no safe approach.
    • vadanaiḥ — by mouths
      Instrumental plural of vadana. The mouths are now the instruments of the cosmic operation. In verses 10–11 they were ornaments of the body; here they are tools of consumption.
    • jvaladbhiḥ — blazing
      Instrumental plural participle of jval. Mouths that blaze even as they devour — fire and consumption are one act, not two.
    • pratapanti — they scorch
      Third-person plural of pra-tap, 'to burn with heat.' Verbal cousin of tejas (radiance). The cosmic radiance and the cosmic scorching are the same energy seen from two angles.
    O Viṣṇu, I see You devouring all people from all sides with Your flaming mouths. Covering all the universe with Your effulgence, You are manifest with terrible, scorching rays.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण
    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.
    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    The yaṅ-form 'lelihyase' — 'You lick again and again' — gives a visceral image of cosmic mastication. The same radiance that filled the heavens with light (11.12) now scorches the worlds with heat. Splendor and consumption are revealed as one act.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The frequentative verb is the chapter's most visceral verb-choice — Sanskrit's grammar itself enacts the repeating-action of devouring. The vocative 'Viṣṇu' (the preserver) used at the climax of destruction-imagery presses the paradox: preservation by the same fire that destroys. This forces Arjuna's question in 11.31.

    Translation
    30. Swallowing all these men all around with Your fiery mouths, You are licking Your lips repeatedly. O Viṣṇu, Your fierce rays, filling the whole universe with their splendor, are burning it up.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    30. Swallowing all these men all around with Your fiery mouths, You are licking Your lips repeatedly. O Viṣṇu, Your fierce rays, filling the whole universe with their heat, are burning it up.
    Commentary

    Having described how the warriors enter the mouths of the universal form, Arjuna describes the effulgence coming from the form and how it spreads out. You swallow with Your fiery mouths all of them who entered swiftly, and lick your lips stained with their blood repeatedly in fury (samantāt). Your intense rays fill up and completely burn the universe with their intolerable heat. O Viṣṇu, You are spread through the universe! It is impossible to flee from You.

    Theme

    Now Arjuna describes Kala-rupa

    COMMON THEME: Text 11.19 marks the beginning of description of ‘Kala-rupa’ (The form as Time) which

    continues up till Text 11.31

    PLEASE NOTE: All points of the purports are included as the sub-points; as such there are no individual ‘Focus of

    Learning’ sections for these verses.

    

    

    ARJUNA’S FURTHER DESCRIPTION OF THE UNIVERSAL FORM AS ‘KALA-RUPA’.

    Blazing fire coming forth from your mouth, burning this entire universe (11.19)
    Numberless arms and sun and moon are the eyes
    Without origin, middle and end
    Repetition of glories is not a flaw – It is a sign of bewilderment, wonder or great ecstasy
    Spread throughout – Spread throughout the sky and planets and all space in between; and all the planetary systems are perturbed seeing you (11.20)
    ‘Dyav-a-prthivyoh’ (Space between heaven and earth) and ‘Loka-trayam’ (Three worlds) –indicate that not only Arjuna saw, but other planetary systems, whoever endowed with divine vision, also saw this form and got perturbed
    This proves that Arjuna’s seeing was not a dream
    Petitioned by demigods – Kala-rupa is petitioned by demigods and sages – All are fearful (11.21 – 11.22)
    Demigods are surrendering and praying with folded hands
    Great sages are praying with Vedic hymns
    Siva, Adityas, Vasus etc beholding You in wonder
    Rasa changes to fear – Arjuna experiences a terrible fearsome sight (11.23)
    Arjuna loses steadiness and equilibrium of mind, because mind is perturbed by fear (11.24)
    Arjuna sees blazing death-like faces and awful teeth (11.25)
    Link between texts 11.25 & 11.26: Text 11.26 through 11.30 describe future occurrences that Arjuna sees within the kala-rupa. In Text 11.7, Krishna said that Arjuna could see “whatever *he+ may want to see in the future.” In these texts, Arjuna sees that Bhisma, Drona and Karna – the three most feared members of the opposing army – will be destroyed.
    Two Analogies: Devouring all soldiers of both armies on both sides, including Bhisma, Drona & Karna, rushing into Your mouth (11.26 – 11.27)
    Analogy: As many waves of river flow into the ocean (11.28)
    Analogy: As moths dash to destruction in blazing fire (11.29*)
    Indicates that Arjuna could see his awaited victory
    All-devouring – You are devouring all people from all sides, your effulgence is covering all the universe with terrible scorching rays(11.30)

    ARJUNA’S QUESTIONS

    Arjuna in great fear asks two questions (11.31)
    Who are You?
    What is Your mission?
    Why Arjuna asks these questions – Because although Arjuna knew Krishna as his friend and Supreme Personality of Godhead, but he was puzzled by various forms exhibited by Krishna

    Personal Guidance
    You lick Your lips, devouring all the worlds with Your blazing mouths — Your terrible rays burn the whole universe.
    Practical Applications
    • Receive the devouring aspect of time/cosmos as Kṛṣṇa's truth.
    • Don't sanitize destruction out of theology.
    • Honor the cosmic accountability.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I sanitized cosmic accountability?
    • What does honoring it require?
    Analogy

    A lion licking its lips after the kill is satisfied; a fire licking the next branch is preparing the next consumption. The Lord's lelihyase is the second image, not the first — He does not rest after eating; the eating itself is continuous, an ongoing function of cosmic time.

    Important Words
    • ākhyāhi — tell
      Imperative of ā-khyā, 'to declare.' Arjuna is not asking for explanation; he is asking for declaration. Identity, stated plainly.
    • ugra - rūpaḥ — of fierce form
      Compound: ugra (fierce) + rūpa (form). Arjuna now names the form by its terrible aspect rather than by its splendor — a shift from verse 17's tejaḥ-rāśim.
    • deva - vara — O greatest of the gods
      Vocative compound. Even in fear, Arjuna keeps the polite form of address. Terror does not erase courtesy in the Gītā's etiquette.
    • prasīda — be gracious
      Same imperative as 11.25. Repeated petitions across the chapter — the verb of begging-for-grace returns and returns.
    • ādyam — the primal
      Accusative of ādya, 'first.' Arjuna recognises the form as primal — before which there is no prior, and therefore no other source of meaning. To know the primal is to know the rest derivatively.
    • pravṛttim — mission, activity
      Accusative of pravṛtti — 'engagement, undertaking.' Arjuna asks not just who but what-for. The Lord's pravṛtti is what the next verse will answer: kālo 'smi.
    O Lord of lords, so fierce of form, please tell me who You are. I offer my obeisances unto You; please be gracious to me. You are the primal Lord. I want to know about You, for I do not know what Your mission is.

    How Sanskrit scholars read this verse — split, rearranged, grammar-tagged. For the plain English distilled meaning, jump to Plain meaning below.
    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    The pivotal question of the chapter: 'Who are You, in this fierce form? What is Your mission?' Arjuna asked to see; now he asks to understand what he is seeing. The reply will be the kāla-asmi verse — the chapter's metaphysical center.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The question 'kaḥ bhavān' is striking — Arjuna has been with Kṛṣṇa his whole life, has just heard ch. 10 declaring identity, yet the ugra-rūpa renders him unfamiliar. 'Pravṛtti' is precisely 'undertaking, what You are setting out to do' — Arjuna is asking after Kṛṣṇa's purpose, not just His identity. The setup is exact: Kṛṣṇa will answer with both.

    O best of gods, tell me: who are You of this fierce form? Salutations to You — be gracious! I wish to know You, the primal one; for I do not understand Your activity.

    Translation
    31. Tell me who You are, with this terrifying form. I offer respects to You. O best of the devas, be merciful to me. I desire to know You, the first being. I do not understand Your purpose.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    31. Tell me who You are, with this terrifying form. I offer respects to You. O bestower of boons, be merciful to me. I desire to know You, the first being. I do not understand Your action.
    Commentary

    After describing the Lord in His universal form equipped with His time energy, Arjuna, knowing the truth of this form, asks about this form, in order to strengthen His knowledge of the matter. Arjuna had requested the Lord to see that form of power endowed with a thousand heads (verse 3). The Lord showed that form, and then He shows that same form as the most ferocious destroyer. Tell me who You are in that ferocious form. O best deity (devavara)! I offer respects to You. Be merciful, and give up that terrible form. I desire to know You, the first being, particularly (vijṣātum). I do not understand Your action—why have you done this? Tell me the purpose.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Arjuna is asking two questions: (1) who are You? and (2) what is Your mission? And Krsna answers:

    [C. "KALO'SMI LOKA‑KSAYA‑KRT" ‑ BECOME MY INSTRUMENT (11. 32‑34) Krsna answers: 'Time I am, destroyer of the world. The great warriors no both sides are already slain by my plan. You can be but an instrument. Arise and fight!"]

    Two Analogies: Devouring all soldiers of both armies on both sides, including Bhisma, Drona & Karna, rushing into Your mouth (11.26 – 11.27)
    Analogy: As many waves of river flow into the ocean (11.28)
    Analogy: As moths dash to destruction in blazing fire (11.29*)
    Indicates that Arjuna could see his awaited victory
    All-devouring – You are devouring all people from all sides, your effulgence is covering all the universe with terrible scorching rays(11.30)

    ARJUNA’S QUESTIONS

    Arjuna in great fear asks two questions (11.31)
    Who are You?
    What is Your mission?
    Why Arjuna asks these questions – Because although Arjuna knew Krishna as his friend and Supreme Personality of Godhead, but he was puzzled by various forms exhibited by Krishna
    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical

    11.31 Akhyahi, tell; me; kah, who; bhavan, You are; ugrarupah, fierce in form. Namah, salutation; astu, be; te, to You; deva-vara, O supreme God, foremost among the gods. Prasida, be gracious. Icchami, I desire; vijnatum, to fully know; bhavantam, You; adyam, who are the Primal One, who exist in the beginning. Hi, for; na prajanami, I do not understand; tava, Your; pravrttim, actions!
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.31 Who are You of this terrible form, what do You intend to do? I wish to know. For I do not know Your intended actions. Tell me this. Salutations to You, O Supreme God! Salutations to You, Lord of everything! Say with what object and for what purpose You have assumed this form of the destroyer. Assume a pleasing form. The Lord, the charioteer of Arjuna, being estioned, 'What is Your intention in assuming a terrible form when revealing Your cosmic sovereignty out of overflowing love for Your proteges?' - He spoke to the following effect: The manifestation of a terrible form by Me is to point out that I Myself am operative for the annihilation of the entire world of kings headed by the sons of Dhrtarastra, without any effort on your (Arjuna's) part. Reminding Arjuna of this, is to goad him to fight:
    Śrī Abhinavagupta Classical

    Personal Guidance
    Tell me who You are, with so terrible a form? I do not understand Your purpose — please be merciful.
    Practical Applications
    • Voice the question rather than freeze in confusion.
    • Ask for the Lord's purpose to be revealed.
    • Honor the right to ask.
    Reflection Questions
    • What confusion have I been freezing in?
    • What asking would unfreeze?
    Analogy

    A petitioner who has been struck dumb by the king's full regalia finally finds his voice and asks the one honest question: 'Sir, who are you, and what do you intend?' Arjuna's question is the question every soul must one day put to the Lord — directly, naming the fear, not pretending to be unafraid.

    Stories
    Prahlāda Asking Nṛsiṁha to Be Pacified

    After Hiraṇyakaśipu's death (SB 7.9), the demigods were too afraid to approach the still-raging Nṛsiṁha. Even Lakṣmī hung back. Only the boy Prahlāda was sent forward, and he prostrated himself and prayed — asking the Lord to please be pacified (prasīda).

    Arjuna's prasīda in 11.31 stands in this lineage. The Lord's fierce form requires not flattery but the honest petition of a devotee who has nowhere else to go.

    Section 3 (11.32–11.34)
    “TIME I AM, BECOME MY INSTRUMENT”
    Section overview
    Krishna replies, “Time I am, the destroyer of the world. The great warriors on both sides are already slain by My plan. You can be but an instrument. Arise and fight!”

    PRACTICAL APPLICATION OF TEXT 11.32 – 11.34

    As the Supersoul, Lord Krishna controls all cosmic events according to His will
    As Time, He is pushing all things towards destruction

    Important Words
    • kālaḥ — Time
      Nominative — and one of the most consequential single words Kṛṣṇa speaks in the Gītā. He identifies Himself not as a god above time but as Time itself. The Bhāgavatam will later devote entire books to expanding this declaration.
    • asmi — I am
      First-person singular of as. Two-word self-identification: kālo 'smi. The form of the great I-am statements that punctuate chapters 7, 9, 10, and 15.
    • kṣaya - kṛt — the destroyer
      Compound: kṣaya (decay) + kṛt (doer). The agent-noun for the active wasting-away of things. Time is not passive decay; it is active doing.
    • pravṛddhaḥ — grown fully
      Past participle of pra-vṛdh, 'to grow completely.' Time has come to its full strength at this moment of the war. The verb implies that destruction is in its appointed season.
    • samāhartum — to engage in destruction
      Infinitive of sam-ā-hṛ, 'to draw together and take.' Even destruction is a gathering — the Lord is collecting what is His.
    • ṛte — except for
      Indeclinable — 'apart from.' Even without Arjuna's action, the result will occur. Arjuna is offered a part, not the only part.
    The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: Time I am, the great destroyer of the worlds, and I have come here to destroy all people. With the exception of you [the Pāṇḍavas], all the soldiers here on both sides will be slain.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण

    Auto-generated study layers — original analysis of the public-domain śloka. Review against a published edition for academic work.
    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    Kṛṣṇa answers: 'I am Time, swollen, destroyer of worlds.' The fierce form is not a side-aspect — it is His identity as cosmic time-process. Whether or not Arjuna fights, the warriors before him are already on their way out. His action neither causes nor prevents.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    The most famous verse of the chapter — quoted by J. Robert Oppenheimer at Trinity. 'Kālaḥ asmi' identifies Kṛṣṇa with kāla, the principle that ripens and reaps every being. The argument is liberating, not crushing: Arjuna's anguish in ch. 1 over killing kinsmen presupposed that his fighting decided their deaths. The cosmic vision shows him that death is already underway by another agent.

    Purport

    Although Arjuna knew that Kṛṣṇa was his friend and the Supreme Personality of Godhead, he was puzzled by the various forms exhibited by Kṛṣṇa. Therefore he asked further about the actual mission of this devastating force. It is written in the Vedas that the Supreme Truth destroys everything, even the brāhmaṇas. As stated in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (1.2.25), yasya brahma ca kṣatraṁ ca ubhe bhavata odanaḥ mṛtyur yasyopasecanaṁ ka itthā veda yatra saḥ Eventually all the brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas and everyone else are devoured like a meal by the Supreme. This form of the Supreme Lord is the all-devouring giant, and here Kṛṣṇa presents Himself in that form of all-devouring time. Except for a few Pāṇḍavas, everyone who was present on that battlefield would be devoured by Him. Arjuna was not in favor of the fight, and he thought it was better not to fight; then there would be no frustration. In reply, the Lord is saying that even if he did not fight, every one of them would be destroyed, for that was His plan. If Arjuna stopped fighting, they would die in another way. Death could not be checked, even if he did not fight. In fact, they were already dead. Time is destruction, and all manifestations are to be vanquished by the desire of the Supreme Lord. That is the law of nature.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    32. The Lord said: I am time, the destroyer of the worlds. Increasing in power, I am here engaged in destroying these men. Even without You, all these warriors arrayed in confronting armies will cease to be.
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    32. The Lord said: I am time, the destroyer of the worlds. Spread everywhere, I am here engaged in destroying these men. Other than you, all these warriors arrayed in confronting armies will not exist in the future.
    Commentary

    Being implored, the Lord answers. I am time, the destroyer of the worlds. I am spread everywhere (pravṛddhaḥ). yasya brahma ca kṣatraṁ ca ubhe bhavata odanaḥ mṛtyur yasyopasecanaṁ ka itthā veda yatra saḥ Who knows the Lord, for whom the brāhmaṇas and kṣatriyas are His food and death is the sauce? Kaṭha Upaniṣad .2.25 I am glorified in this verse as time. Understand that action—at the proper time (iha), I will be engaged in swallowing, in destroying Duryodhana and others. And know the result of that action—except for you, Yudiṣṭhira and a few others, all will not live. Another meaning is derived by taking this verse as a response to the Arjuna supposedly asking, “If I give up the fight, how will they be destroyed?” Even without you fighting, they will be killed. In the form of time, I will take away their lifespan. Who are all those who will be killed? All those troops situated on both sides beginning with Bhīṣma will be killed. But you, if you give up the battle, will have deviated from your dharma.

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Srila Prabhupada explains is his Purport: "Eventually all the brahmanas, ksatriyas and everyone else are devoured like a meal by the Supreme. This form of the Supreme Lord is the all‑ devouring giant, and here Krsna presents Himself in that form of all‑devouring time. Except for a few Pandavas, everyone who was present on that battlefield would be devoured by Him. Arjuna was not in favor of the fight, and he thought it was better not to fight; then there would be no frustration. In reply, the Lord is saying that even if he did not fight, every one of them would be destroyed, for that was His plan. If Arjuna stopped fighting, they would die in another way. Death could not be checked, even if he did not fight. In fact, they were already dead. Time is destruction, and all manifestations are to be vanquished by the desire of the Supreme Lord. That is the law of nature." Whether Arjuna would fight or not, all would be killed. But if Arjuna would not fight he would be the looser ‑ he would loose his religious principles.

    Theme

    Krishna in the form of Universal Time replies to Arjuna’s two questions

    “Time I am” (Kala-rupa)
    Mission – To destroy everything – “All the people in all the worlds, except Pandavas”
    Indicates – Even if Arjuna did not want to fight, they will die anyway
    Ref. Katha Upanisad – All brahmanas, ksatriyas and everyone else are devoured like a meal by the Supreme as the All-devouring giant

    Personal Guidance
    I am terrible time, the destroyer of worlds, here engaged in destroying all — even without you, all these warriors will die.
    Practical Applications
    • Recognize time as Kṛṣṇa's specific manifestation.
    • Don't fight time; align with it.
    • Use mortality as motivation, not despair.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I fighting time?
    • What alignment would free me?
    Analogy

    The clock on the wall is the most unhurried thing in the room and the most relentless. It does not run after anyone. It simply is the passing — and what is passing eventually ends. Kṛṣṇa names Himself as that clock at the heart of the universe.

    Stories
    The Vow of the Pāṇḍavas Already Underway

    Long before this moment on the battlefield, in the assembly hall after the dice-game (Mahābhārata, Sabhā-parva 71–72), Bhīma had vowed to break Duryodhana's thigh, and Draupadī had vowed to remain uncombed until her dishonor was avenged. The deaths of the Kaurava chiefs were already pledged into the cosmic ledger years before any arrow flew.

    Kṛṣṇa's words in 11.32 — ṛte 'pi tvāṁ na bhaviṣyanti — only ratify what was already so. The vows of saintly persons, the curse of Gāndhārī, the arithmetic of adharma had all converged. Time was simply executing what had been written.

    O Savyasācī .
    Important Words
    • uttiṣṭha — stand up
      Imperative of ud-sthā. The same verb Kṛṣṇa used in 2.3 (kṣudraṁ hṛdaya-daurbalyaṁ tyaktvottiṣṭha) — the Gītā returns to this command at its decisive moments. Standing is not metaphor; it is the body's signal of resolve.
    • yaśaḥ — fame
      Accusative of yaśas — glory of right action. Kṛṣṇa offers Arjuna fame not as flattery but as a side-effect of dharma performed in time.
    • nihatāḥ — slain
      Past participle of ni-han, 'to strike down.' Past tense, not future. The killing has occurred at the cosmic level; only the visible enactment remains.
    • pūrvam eva — already, beforehand
      Adverbial phrase — 'precisely before.' Eva intensifies pūrvam. The intensifier closes any escape from the temporal verdict.
    • nimitta - mātram — merely an instrument
      Compound: nimitta (efficient cause) + mātra (mere). One of the Gītā's signature phrases for kartṛtva — Arjuna is the efficient cause, but only as instrument; the real doer is elsewhere.
    • savya - sācin — ambidextrous archer
      Vocative — Arjuna's epithet for being able to shoot equally well with both hands. Kṛṣṇa names him by his unique martial qualification at the moment of asking him to act — addressing the warrior in his strength-name.
    Therefore get up. Prepare to fight and win glory. Conquer your enemies and enjoy a flourishing kingdom. They are already put to death by My arrangement, and you, O Savyasācī, can be but an instrument in the fight.
    Classical Sanskrit analysis शास्त्रीय विश्लेषण

    Plain meaning (तात्पर्य · Tātparya)
    The doctrinal corollary of 11.32: act, but as instrument (nimitta-mātra), not as cause. Glory, victory, kingdom — these still belong to Arjuna in the war; but the metaphysics has been transformed. Killing has been redefined as cooperating with kāla.
    Further notes (विवरण · Vivaraṇa)
    'Nimitta-mātra' becomes one of the Gītā's most consequential phrases for karmayoga. The instrument-ontology dissolves the killer-victim binary that paralyzed Arjuna in ch. 1. The vocative 'Savya-sācin' (one who shoots with either hand) compliments his uniqueness as a warrior — the work is too important to refuse, but his self-conception must change.
    Prose order (अन्वय · Anvaya)

    Therefore stand up, win glory; conquering the enemies, enjoy a flourishing kingdom. These have already been struck down by Me — be a mere instrument, O left-handed archer.

    Purport

    Savya-sācin refers to one who can shoot arrows very expertly in the field; thus Arjuna is addressed as an expert warrior capable of delivering arrows to kill his enemies. “Just become an instrument”: nimitta-mātram. This word is also very significant. The whole world is moving according to the plan of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Foolish persons who do not have sufficient knowledge think that nature is moving without a plan and all manifestations are but accidental formations. There are many so-called scientists who suggest that perhaps it was like this, or maybe like that, but there is no question of “perhaps” and “maybe.” There is a specific plan being carried out in this material world. What is this plan? This cosmic manifestation is a chance for the conditioned souls to go back to Godhead, back to home. As long as they have the domineering mentality which makes them try to lord it over material nature, they are conditioned. But anyone who can understand the plan of the Supreme Lord and cultivate Kṛṣṇa consciousness is most intelligent. The creation and destruction of the cosmic manifestation are under the superior guidance of God. Thus the Battle of Kurukṣetra was fought according to the plan of God. Arjuna was refusing to fight, but he was told that he should fight in accordance with the desire of the Supreme Lord. Then he would be happy. If one is in full Kṛṣṇa consciousness and his life is devoted to the Lord’s transcendental service, he is perfect.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    33. Therefore rise and gain fame. Conquering the enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom. These have all been killed by Me already. Just be an instrument, O Arjuna!
    Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa Gauḍīya
    Translation
    33. Therefore rise and gain fame. Conquering the enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom. These have all been killed by Me already. Just be an instrument, O Arjuna!
    Commentary

    Because of this, rise, and fight according to your dharma. Gain fame. Attain rare glory. Warriors such as Bhīṣma who cannot be conquered by the devas, have been defeated by Arjuna with ease! Such will be your fame. They have already been killed by Me, at the time of their offending Draupadī. They are proceeding like puppets to give you fame. Therefore, just become the instrument. O Arjuna, skilful with the left hand! You are skilful at shooting arrows with your left hand. Therefore at time of battle, you can shoot showers of arrows with both hands!

    Bhūrijana Dāsa Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    'Savyasaci', 'one who can fight with either hand.' Krsna is telling Arjuna to use all his skills now, stand up and fight! That is what Krsna has been telling Arjuna all the time: "Do your duties, stand up and fight!"

    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    Savyasācī also means “one who can fight ambidexterously, with either hand, left or right.” Kṛṣṇa

    therefore encourages Arjuna to now use all his skills to fight, without pride, because pūrvam eva,

    “by previous arrangement,” not because of Arjuna’s skills, the warriors are as good as dead.

    Classical Ācāryas
    Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.33 Tasmat, therefore; tvam, you; uttistha, rise up; (and) labhasva, gain; the yasah, fame, that Arjuna has conered the Atirathas [Atiratha-see note under 1.4.6.-Tr.], Bhisma, Drona and others, who are unconerable even by the gods. Such fame can be acired only by virtuous actions. Jitva, by defeating; satrun, the enemies, Duryodhana and others; bhunksva, enjoy; a rajyam, kingdom; that is samrddham, propersous, free from enemies and obstacles. Ete, these; nihatah, have been definitely killed, made lifeless; eva maya, verily by Me; eva purvam, even earlier. Bhava, be you; nimitta-matram, merely an instrument, O Savyasachin. Arjuna was called so because he could shoot arrows even with his left hand.
    Śrī Rāmānujācārya Classical
    Translation
    11.33 Therefore, arise for fighting against them. Conering your enemies, win glory and enjoy a prosperous and righteous kingdom. All those who have sinned have been already annihilated by Me. Be you merely an instrument (Nimitta) of Mine in destroying them - just like a weapon in my hand, O Savyasacin! The root 'Sac' means 'fastening'. A 'savyasacin' is one who is capable of fixing or fastening the arrow even with his left hand. The meaning is that he is so dexterous that he can fight with a bow in each hand.
